Chapter 2 Stress and equilibrium

2.8 When forces do not turn a body

By definition 2.3, equilibrium of a body has two parts. The resultant of the forces on the body must be the zero vector, and the forces must not tend to turn the body. We wrote the first part with numbers in (2.2) and applied it in section 2.7 to a small cube, which gave the equilibrium equations. The second part is still written only in words. Three things wait for it. The ruler in figure 2.7 turns although the resultant of the forces on it is zero. For pure shear in section 2.6.6 we promised to show why the forces on the four faces of the cube must be equally large. And at the end of the same section a question remained: how does the second condition of equilibrium relate the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\)?

In this section we write the second condition of equilibrium with numbers and derive from it that at every interior point of a body where the stress varies smoothly \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\). The route is this. First we need a quantity that says about which axis a force turns a body and how strongly. It will be a vector along the axis. The axis is perpendicular to the force, so we need a new operation that makes from two vectors a vector perpendicular to both. For it we also need an agreement on how the axes of a coordinate system are placed in space. Then we test the second condition on the ruler. Finally we cut a small cube out of a body in thought and show that it is in equilibrium only if the shear components of stress are equal in pairs.

2.8.1 Mathematics: the vector product

Let us return to the door in figure 2.5, right, which we see from above. The door turns about a vertical axis through the hinge, while the force at the handle is horizontal. The segment from the hinge to the handle is horizontal too. Both lie in the plane of the figure, while the axis points out of the figure and is only a point at the hinge there. So the axis about which the force turns the door is perpendicular to the force and to the segment from the axis to the point where the force acts. How strongly the force turns the door we describe with a number, the axis of the turn with a direction. Together they are a vector along the axis. So we need a rule that makes from two vectors a third one, perpendicular to both. The scalar product of section 2.3 cannot do this, since its result is a number.

The rule that makes a third vector from two vectors is the second part of Hamilton's product from section 2.3. There we saw that the product of the vectors \(a_{\mathrm{x}} i + a_{\mathrm{y}} j + a_{\mathrm{z}} k\) and \(b_{\mathrm{x}} i + b_{\mathrm{y}} j + b_{\mathrm{z}} k\) contains, besides the number, terms with \(i\), \(j\) and \(k\), and that \(ij = k\) and \(ji = -k\). The units \(i\) and \(j\) are unit vectors along the axes \(x\) and \(y\), and \(k\) along the axis \(z\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 156-157). The product of the units along the axes \(x\) and \(y\) is therefore the unit along the axis \(z\), which is perpendicular to both. Exchanging the order reverses the direction. Of the two opposite directions perpendicular to both vectors, one is thus chosen by the order of the factors.

From history

A similar product was also developed by Grassmann (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 158), and Gibbs wrote it with the sign \(\times\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 158), as we do too.

Two nonzero vectors that do not point in the same or in opposite directions have two opposite directions perpendicular to both. For the door the axis of the turn points up or down. Which of the two directions we choose is an agreement, and this agreement is tied to how the axes of the coordinate system are placed in space. Definition 1.12 only requires the axes to be pairwise perpendicular and each to have a chosen positive direction. Once the axes \(x\) and \(y\) are placed, the positive axis \(z\) can point to one side or to the other of the plane in which they lie (figure 2.97). Both systems satisfy the definition, but each is the mirror image of the other, like a right and a left hand.

Definition 2.32 Right-handed coordinate system (desnosučni koordinatni sistem)

A rectangular Cartesian coordinate system is right-handed (desnosučni) when the positive directions of the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), in this order, point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand, spread so that they are pairwise perpendicular. When the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the left hand point like this, the system is left-handed (levosučni).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3, Figs. 186 and 188 (PDF p. 395), BOWER Appendix A.1.3 (PDF p. 739).

Every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system is of one of the two kinds. When we point the thumb and the index finger of the right hand along the positive axes \(x\) and \(y\), the middle finger points to one side of the plane of these two axes. If the positive axis \(z\) points to the same side, the system is right-handed. Otherwise it points to the opposite side, where the middle finger of the left hand points when its thumb and index finger are held the same way, and the system is left-handed. We can also check the difference without hands (figure 2.97). We look from the tip of the positive axis \(z\) toward the origin and turn the positive axis \(x\) by a quarter turn into the positive axis \(y\). In a right-handed system we see this turn counterclockwise, in a left-handed one clockwise. KREYSZIG says the same with a right-handed screw: if we turn it from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), it advances in the direction of the positive axis \(z\) (KREYSZIG §9.3, Fig. 187, PDF p. 395).

We cannot read off right-handedness from components. In both systems of figure 2.97 the unit vectors of the axes have the components \((1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\). The two systems differ in how they are placed in the space they describe, not in the numbers. KREYSZIG uses the same notion for any three vectors, not only for the unit vectors of perpendicular axes, and calls a triple of vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) right-handed when, in this order, they point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand (KREYSZIG §9.3, PDF p. 395). The definition with numbers that we will use, we will give in section 2.10.

The system in figure 1.57 and the system of the sheared cube in figure 1.92 are right-handed. As announced in chapter 1, a coordinate system in this book is always right-handed, unless we say otherwise. We have already met one exception. In part 2 of the proof of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26) we reversed every axis along which the normal has a negative component. Reversing a single axis turns a right-handed system into a left-handed one, as figure 2.97 shows for the axis \(z\). It did no harm there, because that proof does not use the operation we introduce now.

Now let us look for a vector perpendicular to two given vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). We start with a simple case, where both lie in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) and \(\vek b = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). Every vector of the form \((0, 0, c)\) is perpendicular to both, since

\[(a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\cdot(0, 0, c) = a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 0 + a_{\mathrm{y}} \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot c = 0 ,\]

and the same for \(\vek b\). Which number \(c\) should we choose? Let the length of the new vector tell us something about the vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\), for example the area of the parallelogram they span when drawn from the same point (figure 2.101). For \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) on the axis \(x\) the parallelogram has the base \(|a_{\mathrm{x}}|\) and the height \(|b_{\mathrm{y}}|\), the distance of the tip of \(\vek b\) from the axis \(x\). By the school formula its area is the base times the height, \(|a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}}|\). For any two vectors in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) the area is \(|a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}|\), which we will show below. So we choose

\[c = a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

The sign of the number \(c\) tells to which side of the plane the new vector points. For \(\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek b = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) we get \(c = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0 = 1\), and the new vector is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and the new vector then point, in this order, like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand, because the system is right-handed.

For vectors with three components we keep this formula for the component \(z\). The formulas for the components \(x\) and \(y\) we get by exchanging the letters in the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\). From \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\) for the component \(z\) this gives \(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\) for the component \(x\), and from that \(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\) for the component \(y\). That the vector obtained in this way is indeed perpendicular to both we prove in the lemma below.

Definition 2.33 Vector product (vektorski produkt)

The vector product (vektorski produkt) of the vectors \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\vek b = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{z}})\), written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, is the vector

\[\vek a\times\vek b = (a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}},\ \ a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}},\ \ a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}) . \tag{2.39}\]

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3 (2) (PDF p. 394), CM (2.2.12), (2.2.49), (2.2.52) (PDF pp. 43, 54-55). Both define it by its length and direction and derive the formula with components.

The result is a vector, hence the name. Books also call it the cross product (križni produkt) (KREYSZIG §9.3, PDF p. 394, CM, PDF p. 43). Grassmann called it the external product (zunanji produkt) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 158). Each component is the difference of two products in which only the other two letters appear. In the component \(x\) these are \(y\) and \(z\). KREYSZIG warns that in a left-handed system each component would have to be multiplied by \(-1\) to get the same vector (KREYSZIG §9.3, PDF p. 394). Figure 2.97 shows why. The unit vectors of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) are the same in both systems, and formula (2.39) gives in both \((1, 0, 0)\times(0, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 1)\), the unit vector of the positive axis \(z\). But this one points up in the right-handed system and down in the left-handed one. The same two vectors would thus give opposite vectors by the same formula, depending on the chosen system. That is why we agreed above on right-handed systems.

Let us test the formula on the fly's flight \(\vek a = (1, 2, -2)\) and the vector \(\vek b = (2, -1, 0)\) of section 2.3, which is perpendicular to it. By (2.39)

\[\vek a\times\vek b = \big(2 \cdot 0 - (-2)(-1),\ \ (-2) \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 0,\ \ 1 \cdot (-1) - 2 \cdot 2\big) = (-2, -4, -5) .\]

The scalar products \(\vek a\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = -2 - 8 + 10 = 0\) and \(\vek b\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = -4 + 4 + 0 = 0\) confirm that it is perpendicular to both. Its length is \(\sqrt{4 + 16 + 25} = \sqrt{45}\). Since \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) are perpendicular, their parallelogram is a rectangle with the sides \(|\vek a| = 3\) and \(|\vek b| = \sqrt5\), with the area \(3\sqrt5 = \sqrt{45}\) (figure 2.98). The length of the vector product is indeed the area of the parallelogram. Items 4 and 5 of the next lemma say this in general.

Lemma 2.34 Properties of the vector product (lastnosti vektorskega produkta)

For all vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and all numbers \(k\):

  1. \(\vek b\times\vek a = -(\vek a\times\vek b)\), so \(\vek a\times\vek a = \vek 0\),
  2. \(\vek a\times(\vek b + \vek c) = \vek a\times\vek b + \vek a\times\vek c\) and \((\vek a + \vek b)\times\vek c = \vek a\times\vek c + \vek b\times\vek c\),
  3. \((k\,\vek a)\times\vek b = k\,(\vek a\times\vek b) = \vek a\times(k\,\vek b)\),
  4. \(\vek a\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = 0\) and \(\vek b\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = 0\),
  5. \(|\vek a\times\vek b|^2 = |\vek a|^2\,|\vek b|^2 - (\vek a\cdot\vek b)^2\),
  6. \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Items 2 and 3 are shown by figure 2.99. On the left is the parallelogram of the vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\), and above it the parallelogram of the vectors \(2\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) with a base twice as long and twice the area, so \(|(k\,\vek a)\times\vek b|\) is \(k\) times \(|\vek a\times\vek b|\). On the right we look along the vector \(\vek a\), where the perpendicular components of the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) and their sum form a triangle. The product with \(\vek a\) turns every vector in this plane by a quarter circle and stretches it \(|\vek a|\) times, so the turned vectors \(\vek a\times\vek b\), \(\vek a\times\vek c\) and \(\vek a\times(\vek b + \vek c)\) form a similar triangle, and the third is the sum of the first two.

Proof

We write each rule with components by (2.39) and reduce it to rules for numbers. The components \(y\) and \(z\) in (2.39) arise from the component \(x\) by exchanging the letters in the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\). For items 1 to 3 it is therefore enough to check the component \(x\), because the same computation with exchanged letters gives the other two.

1. Exchanging the order.

  1. By (2.39) the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek b\times\vek a\) is \(b_{\mathrm{y}} a_{\mathrm{z}} - b_{\mathrm{z}} a_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  2. In a product of numbers the order does not matter, so this is \(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} = -(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}})\), the negative of the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a\times\vek b\).
  3. For \(\vek b = \vek a\) we get \(\vek a\times\vek a = -(\vek a\times\vek a)\). Every component \(q\) of this vector satisfies \(q = -q\), so \(2q = 0\) and \(q = 0\). Therefore \(\vek a\times\vek a = \vek 0\).

2. Splitting a sum.

  1. The sum \(\vek b + \vek c\) has the components \(b_{\mathrm{x}} + c_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(b_{\mathrm{y}} + c_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{z}} + c_{\mathrm{z}}\) (definition 1.14), so the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a\times(\vek b + \vek c)\) is \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\,(b_{\mathrm{z}} + c_{\mathrm{z}}) - a_{\mathrm{z}}\,(b_{\mathrm{y}} + c_{\mathrm{y}})\).
  2. We multiply out the brackets and rearrange the terms into \((a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}}) + (a_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{y}})\). This is the sum of the components \(x\) of the vectors \(\vek a\times\vek b\) and \(\vek a\times\vek c\).
  3. The second equality follows from item 1, the first equality and item 1 once more:
    \[(\vek a + \vek b)\times\vek c = -\big(\vek c\times(\vek a + \vek b)\big) = -(\vek c\times\vek a) - (\vek c\times\vek b) = \vek a\times\vek c + \vek b\times\vek c .\]

3. Taking out a number.

  1. The vector \(k\,\vek a\) has the components \(k a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(k a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(k a_{\mathrm{z}}\), so the component \(x\) of the vector \((k\,\vek a)\times\vek b\) is \((k a_{\mathrm{y}})\,b_{\mathrm{z}} - (k a_{\mathrm{z}})\,b_{\mathrm{y}} = k\,(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}})\). This is the component \(x\) of the vector \(k\,(\vek a\times\vek b)\).
  2. In the same way the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a\times(k\,\vek b)\) is \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\,(k b_{\mathrm{z}}) - a_{\mathrm{z}}\,(k b_{\mathrm{y}}) = k\,(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}})\).

4. Perpendicularity.

  1. By (2.6) and (2.39)
    \[\vek a\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = a_{\mathrm{x}}\,(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}}) + a_{\mathrm{y}}\,(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}}) + a_{\mathrm{z}}\,(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}) .\]
  2. We multiply out the brackets and group the terms in pairs that cancel:
    \[(a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}}) + (-a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}}) + (a_{\mathrm{y}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}) = 0 .\]
  3. For perpendicularity to \(\vek b\) we exchange the roles of the vectors. By item 1, \(\vek a\times\vek b = -(\vek b\times\vek a)\), so \(\vek b\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = -\,\vek b\cdot(\vek b\times\vek a)\) (lemma 2.12, item 3). This is zero by steps 1 and 2.

5. Length.

  1. By (1.10) the square of the length of the vector product is the sum of the squares of the components:
    \[|\vek a\times\vek b|^2 = (a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}})^2 + (a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}})^2 + (a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}})^2 .\]
  2. We expand each square by the school formula for the square of a difference. We get six squares and three double products:
    \[a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 b_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2 b_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2 b_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 b_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 b_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 b_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 2\,a_{\mathrm{y}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - 2\,a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - 2\,a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} .\]
  3. By (1.10), \(|\vek a|^2\,|\vek b|^2 = (a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2)(b_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + b_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + b_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\). Multiplying out, we multiply each term of the first bracket by each term of the second. In figure 2.100, on the left, the terms of the first bracket are written beside the rows, those of the second above the columns, and each product stands in the cell of its row and its column. There are nine cells. The three terms on the diagonal have the same letter twice, \(a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 b_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 b_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2 b_{\mathrm{z}}^2\). The six others have two different letters, and these are the six squares of step 2.
  4. By (2.6) and the school formula for the square of a sum of three numbers,
    \[(\vek a\cdot\vek b)^2 = a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 b_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 b_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2 b_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\,a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\,a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\,a_{\mathrm{y}} a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} .\]
    On the right of the figure is the same table for this square, with the terms \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\) beside the rows and above the columns. Its diagonal gives the same three terms as the left one. Two cells that lie symmetric about the diagonal hold the same product, for example \(a_{\mathrm{x}} a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\), so each such pair gives one double product.
  5. Subtracting \((\vek a\cdot\vek b)^2\) from \(|\vek a|^2\,|\vek b|^2\), the equal diagonals cancel, the three terms with the same letter twice. Six blue cells remain minus six orange cells, and this is the expression of step 2.

6. Unit vectors of the axes.

  1. By (2.39) with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0)\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0) = (0, 0, 1) = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The axes \(x\) and \(y\) give the axis \(z\).
  2. In the same way \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0) = (1, 0, 0) = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1) = (0, 1, 0) = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The same holds around the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3 (3)-(6), Theorem 1 (PDF pp. 396-397), Problem 4, equation (12) (PDF p. 400), CM (2.2.17), (2.2.18) (PDF pp. 44-45), BOWER Appendix A.1.2 (PDF p. 739). KREYSZIG proves the splitting of a sum by components (PDF p. 397), the other proofs are not from the sources.

Items 1 to 3 tell us how to compute with the vector product. We may multiply out brackets and take out numbers as when multiplying numbers, but we may not exchange the order of the factors, because this changes the sign (figure 2.101). Nor may we move the brackets in a product of three factors. By items 1, 3 and 6, for example,

\[(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek 0\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek 0 , \qquad \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\]

(KREYSZIG §9.3 (7), PDF p. 397).

Item 4 says that the vector product is indeed perpendicular to both factors. Item 5 says how long it is. Let us show that this is the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). For \(\vek a = \vek 0\) the parallelogram has area 0, and by item 3 with \(k = 0\) we get \(\vek 0\times\vek b = (0\,\vek a)\times\vek b = 0\,(\vek a\times\vek b) = \vek 0\), so it agrees. Now let \(\vek a \neq \vek 0\) and let \(\vek e = \vek a/|\vek a|\) be the unit vector in its direction. The area of a parallelogram is the base times the height. The base is the side \(\vek a\), with the length \(|\vek a|\). The height \(v\) is the length of the segment that is perpendicular to the line through the side \(\vek a\) and reaches the tip of the vector \(\vek b\). This is the length of the part of the vector \(\vek b\) perpendicular to \(\vek e\), so by item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector \(v^2 = |\vek b|^2 - (\vek b\cdot\vek e)^2\). Since \(\vek b\cdot\vek e = (\vek a\cdot\vek b)/|\vek a|\) by items 1 and 3 of the properties of the scalar product,

\[\big(|\vek a|\,v\big)^2 = |\vek a|^2\left(|\vek b|^2 - \frac{(\vek a\cdot\vek b)^2}{|\vek a|^2}\right) = |\vek a|^2\,|\vek b|^2 - (\vek a\cdot\vek b)^2 = |\vek a\times\vek b|^2 ,\]

the last equality by item 5. Both numbers \(|\vek a|\,v\) and \(|\vek a\times\vek b|\) are nonnegative and have the same square, so by lemma 1.29 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square they are equal. The length of the vector product is therefore the area of the parallelogram. So the length of our vector product agrees with the definitions in KREYSZIG (§9.3 (1), PDF p. 394) and CM (PDF p. 43), which take the length of the vector product to be the area of the parallelogram. For two vectors in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) the vector product is \((0, 0, a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}})\), and its length \(|a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}|\) is the area we promised above. When \(\vek b = k\,\vek a\) points in the direction of the vector \(\vek a\) or opposite to it, the parallelogram is flattened into a segment, and indeed by items 3 and 1, \(\vek a\times(k\,\vek a) = k\,(\vek a\times\vek a) = \vek 0\).

Into which of the two perpendicular directions does the vector product point? In figure 2.101 the vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) are drawn from the point \(O\) in the plane of the page, and the axis \(y\) points into the picture. The product \(\vek a\times\vek b\) points into the picture, the product \(\vek b\times\vek a\) out of it. KREYSZIG and CM say this with the right-hand rule (pravilo desne roke): the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b\), in this order, point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand, or, in other words, a right-handed screw turned from \(\vek a\) toward \(\vek b\) the shorter way advances in the direction of \(\vek a\times\vek b\) (KREYSZIG §9.3, PDF pp. 394-395, CM, PDF p. 43). The sources take the rule as the definition of the direction. For us the direction is fixed by formula (2.39), and the rule is a statement about this formula. For the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) item 6 of the lemma confirms it, since the triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is right-handed by definition 2.32. The right-hand rule describes the position of fingers in space, so we cannot prove it with components until we write it with numbers. We will do so in section 2.10.1, with the sign of a number computed from the components of three vectors, and there we will prove the statement for any vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) with \(\vek a\times\vek b \neq \vek 0\). In our examples the vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) will mostly lie in the plane of two axes, where we can check it directly, as for \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

We put the vector product to use on stress at once. In definition 2.18 we got the shear part of the vector \(\vek t\) by subtraction, as the remainder \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) when the normal part is taken away from the vector \(\vek t\) (figure 2.37). CM writes the same vector with two vector products, as \(\vek n\times(\vek t\times\vek n)\) (CM (4.2.16), PDF p. 184). We will show that this is the same vector as \((\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n\). This form computes the shear part straight from \(\vek n\) and \(\vek t\), without computing the normal stress first, and it tells what the vector product with the normal does to a vector. Why would two vector products give the same as a subtraction? Let us first look at an example with numbers that we chose ourselves, so that the results are round.

Take a plane face through the point \(P\). Let its unit normal and the force per unit area that acts on it be

\[\vek n = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23,\ \tfrac23) , \qquad \vek t = (50,\ 55,\ 10)\ \text{MPa} .\]

Figure 2.102 shows the face on the left, seen obliquely from the side. We drew it in its own position, with the normal up and not in the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), so that the face lies in front of us like a table. The normal is a unit vector, since \(|\vek n|^2 = \tfrac19 + \tfrac49 + \tfrac49 = 1\). We draw the vector \(\vek t\) from the point \(P\). Its length is \(\sqrt{50^2 + 55^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{5625} = 75\) MPa. By (2.11) the normal stress is

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n = 50 \cdot \tfrac13 + 55 \cdot \tfrac23 + 10 \cdot \tfrac23 = 60\ \text{MPa} .\]

The normal part \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = (20, 40, 40)\) MPa is an arrow of length \(60\) MPa along the normal. The shear part we get by subtraction,

\[\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = (50 - 20,\ \ 55 - 40,\ \ 10 - 40) = (30,\ 15,\ -30)\ \text{MPa} .\]

Its length is the shear stress, \(\tau = \sqrt{900 + 225 + 900} = \sqrt{2025} = 45\) MPa. The shear part lies in the face, because it is perpendicular to the normal: \(30 \cdot \tfrac13 + 15 \cdot \tfrac23 - 30 \cdot \tfrac23 = 10 + 10 - 20 = 0\). The arrows \(\vek t\), the normal part and the shear part make a right triangle with the sides \(75\), \(60\) and \(45\) MPa. We see it when we move the shear part up, from the tip of the normal part to the tip of the vector \(\vek t\).

Now let us try the same with the vector product. By (2.39),

\[\vek n\times\vek t = \big(\tfrac23 \cdot 10 - \tfrac23 \cdot 55,\ \ \tfrac23 \cdot 50 - \tfrac13 \cdot 10,\ \ \tfrac13 \cdot 55 - \tfrac23 \cdot 50\big) = (-30,\ 30,\ -15)\ \text{MPa} .\]

What do we know about this vector? By item 4 of lemma 2.34 it is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), so it lies in the face. It is also perpendicular to the shear part, since \((-30) \cdot 30 + 30 \cdot 15 + (-15)(-30) = -900 + 450 + 450 = 0\). Its length is \(\sqrt{900 + 900 + 225} = \sqrt{2025} = 45\) MPa, exactly that of the shear part. So the vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) is the shear part, turned in the face by a quarter turn. It already has the right length, but not yet the right direction. So we multiply it by the normal once more, this time from the right:

\[(\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = \big(30 \cdot \tfrac23 - (-15) \cdot \tfrac23,\ \ (-15) \cdot \tfrac13 - (-30) \cdot \tfrac23,\ \ (-30) \cdot \tfrac23 - 30 \cdot \tfrac13\big) = (30,\ 15,\ -30)\ \text{MPa} .\]

This is exactly the shear part, with the same sign. What the two products did is shown on the right of figure 2.102. There we look at the face from the tip of the normal, so that the normal points at us and we see it only as a dot in a small circle. From there we see the vector \(\vek t\) exactly above the shear part, because its normal part points at us. The first product gave a vector turned from the shear part by a quarter turn counterclockwise. The second product turned it back by a quarter turn, clockwise.

Is this a coincidence of the chosen numbers? It is not. For two vector products in a row there is a rule that turns them into scalar products. Because it holds two vector products, it is called the double vector product (dvojni vektorski produkt), and CM calls it, after the three vectors in it, the "vector triple product" (CM §2.2.2.3, PDF p. 45).

Lemma 2.35 Vector triple product (dvojni vektorski produkt)

For all vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system,

\[(\vek a\times\vek b)\times\vek c = (\vek a\cdot\vek c)\,\vek b - (\vek b\cdot\vek c)\,\vek a . \tag{2.40}\]

For every unit vector \(\vek n\) and every vector \(\vek t\) therefore

\[(\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = \vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n , \qquad |\vek n\times\vek t| = |\vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n| . \tag{2.41}\]
Proof

We check the first equality by components: we write out the left side by (2.39) and collect the terms into scalar products. The other two follow from the first and from properties we already have.

1. The general equality.

  1. Denote the intermediate vector by \(\vek d = \vek a\times\vek b\). By (2.39) its components are \(d_{\mathrm{y}} = a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}} = a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek d\times\vek c\) is \(d_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{z}} - d_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  2. We insert \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\):
    \[d_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{z}} - d_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{y}} = (a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}})\,c_{\mathrm{z}} - (a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}})\,c_{\mathrm{y}} .\]
  3. We multiply out the brackets. The terms with \(b_{\mathrm{x}}\) are \(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{y}}\), the terms with \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\) are \(-a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(-a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}}\). We collect each pair:
    \[b_{\mathrm{x}}\,(a_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}) - a_{\mathrm{x}}\,(b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}} + b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]
    In figure 2.103 the first bracket is the upper row, multiplied by \(b_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the second bracket the lower row, multiplied by \(-a_{\mathrm{x}}\). Each term stands in the column of the letter its two factors share, \(a_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}}\) for example in the column \(y\). In both rows the term in the column \(x\) is missing.
  4. We add the missing terms. We add and subtract the same number \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}}\), once in the first bracket and once in the second. In the first bracket it is the term \(a_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}}\), multiplied by \(b_{\mathrm{x}}\), in the second the term \(b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}}\), multiplied by \(-a_{\mathrm{x}}\). In all we add \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), which does not change the value:
    \[b_{\mathrm{x}}\,(a_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}) - a_{\mathrm{x}}\,(b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}} + b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}} + b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]
  5. By (2.6) the full rows are \(\vek a\cdot\vek c\) and \(\vek b\cdot\vek c\). So the component \(x\) of the left side is \((\vek a\cdot\vek c)\,b_{\mathrm{x}} - (\vek b\cdot\vek c)\,a_{\mathrm{x}}\), and this is the component \(x\) of the right side.
  6. For the components \(y\) and \(z\) we replace the letters in the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\). Formula (2.39) goes into itself and the scalar products keep their value, so the same computation gives them.

2. A unit vector.

  1. In (2.40) we put \(\vek a = \vek n\), \(\vek b = \vek t\) and \(\vek c = \vek n\):
    \[(\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = (\vek n\cdot\vek n)\,\vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n .\]
  2. The vector \(\vek n\) is a unit vector, so \(\vek n\cdot\vek n = |\vek n|^2 = 1\) ((2.6) and (1.10)). This is the first equality in (2.41).
  3. For the length of the vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) we use item 5 of lemma 2.34 with \(|\vek n| = 1\): \(|\vek n\times\vek t|^2 = |\vek n|^2\,|\vek t|^2 - (\vek n\cdot\vek t)^2 = |\vek t|^2 - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)^2\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, also for the remainder \(|\vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n|^2 = |\vek t|^2 - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)^2\).
  5. The lengths \(|\vek n\times\vek t|\) and \(|\vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n|\) are nonnegative and have the same square, so by lemma 1.29, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, they are equal.

Source: CM (2.2.25), (2.2.26) (PDF p. 46), CM (4.2.16) (PDF p. 184). CM states the general equality without proof, the proof by components is not from the sources.

The lemma says that the example was no coincidence. Since \(\vek t\cdot\vek n = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\), for a unit normal the vector \((\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n\) is exactly the shear part \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) of definition 2.18, and the vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) has the length \(\tau\). The proof is a computation with components. Why the two products act as two turns is shown by a triple of vectors that we set on the face.

Definition 2.36 Local triad on a face (lokalna trojica na ploskvi)

Let a force act on a plane face with the unit normal \(\vek n\), equal per unit area to the vector \(\vek t\), and let the shear stress \(\tau\) on this face be different from zero. The shear direction or tangent (tangenta) is the unit vector in the direction of the shear part, and the binormal (binormala) is the vector product of the normal and the tangent:

\[\vek p = \frac{1}{\tau}\,(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n) , \qquad \vek q = \vek n\times\vek p . \tag{2.42}\]

The vectors \(\vek n\), \(\vek p\) and \(\vek q\), in this order, are the local triad (lokalna trojica) of the face for the vector \(\vek t\).

Source: The triad is not from the sources. We built it from definition 2.18 and the vector product. CM draws both parts of the stress vector on a face (CM, Fig. 4.2.5, PDF p. 184).

The name local says that the triad belongs to this face and this vector \(\vek t\), not to the coordinate system. Tangent is the name of a direction that lies in the face, and the binormal is the second direction perpendicular to the tangent, besides the normal (the prefix bi- means two). In figure 2.102 the triad is drawn at the lower left. The normal \(\vek n\) points perpendicularly out of the face. The tangent \(\vek p\) lies in the face and points the same way as the shear part. The binormal \(\vek q\) lies in the face and is perpendicular to the tangent. All three are unit vectors and perpendicular in pairs, and each of these properties we have from before:

  • \(\vek p\) is a unit vector, because we divided the shear part by its length \(\tau\), and it is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), because the shear part is perpendicular to \(\vek n\) (lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector),
  • \(\vek q\) is perpendicular to \(\vek n\) and to \(\vek p\) by item 4 of lemma 2.34,
  • \(\vek q\) is a unit vector by item 5 of the same lemma, \(|\vek q|^2 = |\vek n|^2\,|\vek p|^2 - (\vek n\cdot\vek p)^2 = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 = 1\).

In the example \(\vek p = \tfrac{1}{45}\,(30, 15, -30) = (\tfrac23, \tfrac13, -\tfrac23)\) and \(\vek q = \vek n\times\vek p = (-\tfrac23, \tfrac23, -\tfrac13)\). To which side of the tangent the binormal points is told by the right-hand rule: \(\vek n\), \(\vek p\) and \(\vek q\) point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand, so seen from the tip of the normal the binormal is turned from the tangent by a quarter turn counterclockwise. This is how the figure is drawn. We will prove the right-hand rule in section 2.10.1, and the computation below does not need it.

In the local triad the computation is short, and we see every step in figure 2.102.

  1. By the definition of the tangent the shear part is \(\tau\,\vek p\), so the vector \(\vek t\) is the sum of the normal part and the shear part, \(\vek t = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n + \tau\,\vek p\).
  2. We split the first product by items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.34: \(\vek n\times\vek t = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\,(\vek n\times\vek n) + \tau\,(\vek n\times\vek p)\). By item 1 of the same lemma \(\vek n\times\vek n = \vek 0\), and \(\vek n\times\vek p\) is the binormal, so
    \[\vek n\times\vek t = \tau\,\vek q .\]
    So the product with the normal cut off the normal part and turned the shear part from the direction \(\vek p\) into the direction \(\vek q\). The length did not change, because \(\vek q\) is a unit vector: \(|\vek n\times\vek t| = \tau\).
  3. The second product is \((\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = \tau\,(\vek q\times\vek n)\) by item 3 of the same lemma. By (2.41), in which we take \(\vek p\) in place of \(\vek t\), we have \(\vek q\times\vek n = (\vek n\times\vek p)\times\vek n = \vek p - (\vek p\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n = \vek p\), because \(\vek p\cdot\vek n = 0\). So
    \[(\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = \tau\,\vek p ,\]
    the shear part. The product with the normal from the right turned the vector back from the direction \(\vek q\) into the direction \(\vek p\).

With the numbers of the example: \(\tau\,\vek q\) is \(45 \cdot (-\tfrac23, \tfrac23, -\tfrac13) = (-30, 30, -15)\) MPa and \(\tau\,\vek p\) is \(45 \cdot (\tfrac23, \tfrac13, -\tfrac23) = (30, 15, -30)\) MPa, as above.

The length \(\tau\) can also be read from an angle. In the right triangle on the left of figure 2.102, the angle \(\alpha\) is the angle between the normal and the vector \(\vek t\). The hypotenuse is \(|\vek t|\), and the side opposite the angle \(\alpha\) has the length \(\tau\), so by school trigonometry

\[|\vek n\times\vek t| = \tau = |\vek t|\sin\alpha .\]

In the example \(\cos\alpha = \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}/|\vek t| = 60/75 = 0{,}8\), so \(\alpha = 36{,}87^\circ\) and \(\sin\alpha = 0{,}6\), and indeed \(75 \cdot 0{,}6 = 45\) MPa. For a negative normal stress the angle \(\alpha\) is obtuse, the triangle has the angle \(180^\circ - \alpha\) at the point \(P\), and since \(\sin(180^\circ - \alpha) = \sin\alpha\) (school trigonometry), the formula stays the same. KREYSZIG and CM define the length of the vector product by this formula, \(|\vek a\times\vek b| = |\vek a|\,|\vek b|\sin\gamma\) with the angle \(\gamma\) between the vectors (KREYSZIG §9.3 (1), PDF p. 394, CM (2.2.12), PDF p. 43). In the lectures the normal and the shear part are the vectors \(\vec\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\vec\sigma_{\mathrm{s}}\), the intermediate vectors are \(\vec c = \vec n\times\vec t\) and \(\vec d = \vec c\times\vec n\), and the triple \(\vec n\), \(\vec p\), \(\vec q\) is called an orthonormal basis (ortonormirana baza). Our computation says that \(\vec d = +\vec\sigma_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(|\vec c| = |\vec d| = |\vec\sigma_{\mathrm{s}}|\).

The lemma and the triad have three assumptions. For each let us say why it holds here, when it does not hold and what it does to the result.

  • The normal is a unit vector. Here this holds because the normal is a unit vector by definition 2.17. When a face is given by a vector \(\vek m\) that is perpendicular to it and not a unit vector, (2.40) gives \((\vek m\times\vek t)\times\vek m = |\vek m|^2\,\vek t - (\vek t\cdot\vek m)\,\vek m\). With \(\vek m = |\vek m|\,\vek n\) this is \(|\vek m|^2\,(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n)\), the shear part multiplied by the square of the length of the vector \(\vek m\). For \(\vek m = 2\,\vek n = (\tfrac23, \tfrac43, \tfrac43)\) in the example we get \((120, 60, -120)\) MPa with the length \(180\) MPa instead of \(45\) MPa, four times too much. So we first divide the vector \(\vek m\) by its length, or we divide the result by \(|\vek m|^2\).
  • The coordinate system is right-handed. This assumption does not change the result. In a left-handed system we would, by KREYSZIG, have to multiply every vector product by \(-1\) (KREYSZIG §9.3, PDF p. 394). In \((\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n\) there are two of them, and \((-1) \cdot (-1) = 1\). The right side, \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\), holds no vector product at all. Only the intermediate vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) changes, it would point the opposite way.
  • The shear stress is not zero. Only the local triad needs this, the lemma does not. When \(\vek t\) points along the normal, as on the cross section of the bar with \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = \sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), there is no shear part and the tangent is not determined. Equality (2.41) still holds, since \(\vek n\times\vek t = \sigma\,(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \vek 0\) and both sides are the zero vector.

The order of the factors and the brackets matter. If we multiply the vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) by the normal from the left instead of from the right, item 1 of lemma 2.34 gives

\[\vek n\times(\vek n\times\vek t) = -\big((\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n\big) = -(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n) ,\]

the opposite vector of the shear part, in the example \((-30, -15, 30)\) MPa. On the right of figure 2.102 this means that we would turn the vector \(\vek n\times\vek t\) once more the same way instead of back, by half a turn in all. The form of CM, \(\vek n\times(\vek t\times\vek n)\), is however the same vector as ours. By item 1 of the same lemma \(\vek t\times\vek n = -(\vek n\times\vek t)\), and by item 3 with \(k = -1\) we take this minus out of the product, so

\[\vek n\times(\vek t\times\vek n) = -\big((\vek t\times\vek n)\times\vek n\big) = (\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n .\]

In the first step we swapped the order of the outer product, in the second that of the inner one, and each swap brings one minus.

Let us return once more to the oblique cut of the bar of section 2.4 (figure 2.37), where \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \(\vek t = \sigma\cos\theta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). Both lie in the plane of the figure, so their vector product is perpendicular to the figure and has only the component \(z\):

\[\vek n\times\vek t = (0,\ 0,\ \cos\theta \cdot 0 - \sin\theta \cdot \sigma\cos\theta) = (0,\ 0,\ -\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta) .\]

Its length \(|\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta|\) is the shear stress (2.14), this time in one line. At \(\theta = 30^\circ\) this is \(0{,}433\,|\sigma|\), as in the table of that section. The second product gives

\[(\vek n\times\vek t)\times\vek n = \sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta\,(\sin\theta,\ -\cos\theta,\ 0) ,\]

which is the shear part of step 4 of the derivation there. All numbers of this example and both equalities of the lemma were checked with SymPy.

2.8.2 The moment of a force

From history

A bar with a support, which we push down at one end and so raise a load at the other, is a lever (vzvod). Aristotle knew the property of the lever, but he could not establish its mathematical theory. He described a body at the end of a lever by two motions, one along the tangent to the circle and one along the radius, the first according to nature and the second contrary to nature. In Whewell's opinion such notions did not fit the facts and made it impossible to perceive the true reason for the properties of the lever (CAJORI, PDF p. 53). A small book on mechanics, sometimes ascribed to Aristotle but probably not his (BALL, PDF p. 76), was closer to the truth. It states that what is gained in power is lost in speed, and therefore that two weights which keep a lever in equilibrium are inversely proportional to the arms of the lever. This is why it is easier to extract teeth with a pair of pincers than with the fingers (BALL, PDF p. 77). We see the reason on a lever with arms of 2 m and 1 m (figure 2.104). Turned through the same angle, the end of the longer arm describes an arc twice as long as the end of the shorter one, so the load on the longer arm moves twice as far. What we gain in distance we lose in force, so the weight on the longer arm must be half as large.

A proof of the conditions under which a lever is in equilibrium, which TIMO calls rigorous, was given by Archimedes (287 to 212 BC, TIMO, PDF p. 3). In his work on mechanics he derived it for two weights \(P\) and \(Q\) at the points \(A\) and \(B\) of a light bar. He looked for the point \(O\) of the bar at which we support the bar so that it stays at rest, and he wanted to prove \(P \cdot OA = Q \cdot OB\) (BALL, PDF p. 102). Let us take \(P = 2\), \(Q = 1\), \(A = 0\) and \(B = 3\) (figure 2.105). He replaced the weight \(P\) by a uniformly heavy bar \(LH\) of weight \(P\) with its middle at \(A\), and the weight \(Q\) by a bar \(HK\) of weight \(Q\) with its middle at \(B\). The pull of each weight acts at the point where we hold it, and the weight of a uniform bar acts at its middle, so the replacement does not change the effect. He chose the lengths so that the bars have the same weight per unit length: \(L = -2\), \(H = 2\), \(K = 4\), so \(LH = 4\) and \(HK = 2\), in the ratio \(2 : 1 = P : Q\), and both weigh \(0{,}5\) per unit length. Together they are one uniform bar \(LK\), whose centre of gravity is at its middle \(O = 1\). Indeed \(P \cdot OA = 2 \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 2 = Q \cdot OB\) (BALL, PDF p. 102). With arms in the ratio 1 to 1000, weights in the ratio 1000 to 1 thus balance, and so Archimedes is credited with the saying that with a firm support he could move the whole Earth (BALL, PDF p. 102, CAJORI, PDF p. 53). Mach later objected to the proof that from the mere assumption that equal weights at equal distances are in equilibrium it derives the inverse proportionality of weights and arms (CAJORI, PDF p. 53). In our reading the reason for the objection is the step with the replacement. That the weight of a uniform bar acts like one weight at its middle is a statement of the same kind as the one the proof is looking for.

Statics rested on the theory of the lever of Archimedes until Stevin, of whom we told in section 2.1 (BALL, PDF pp. 102, 274). Galileo wrote down for machines the principle that what we gain in force we lose in speed, in the same ratio (BALL, PDF p. 277). As we saw in chapter 1, he treated a bar built into a wall as a lever about the edge of the wall (TIMO, PDF pp. 19-20). A force turns a body the more strongly, the larger it is and the farther from the support it acts, measured perpendicular to its direction (EP §1.2, p. 8).

Let us return to the door and write down how a force turns a body about a point. With the door in figure 2.5 we saw that the size of the force counts, and how far from the hinge it acts. The vector product captures both.

Definition 2.37 Moment of a force (moment sile)

Let a force \(\vek F\) act at a point \(A\), and let \(O\) be a point. The moment (moment) of the force \(\vek F\) about the point \(O\) is the vector

\[\vek M_{\mathrm{O}} = \vek r\times\vek F , \qquad \vek r = \overrightarrow{OA} , \tag{2.43}\]

where \(\vek r\) is the vector from the point \(O\) to the point \(A\) at which the force acts.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3 (8), Example 3 (PDF p. 397), CM (2.2.9)-(2.2.11) (PDF pp. 42-43).

The vector \(\vek r\) has components in metres and the force in newtons, so by (2.39) every component of the moment has the unit newton metre, N m. The force tends to turn the vector \(\vek r\) toward the direction of the force (CM, PDF pp. 42-43). The moment points along the axis of this turn, by the right-hand rule: \(\vek r\), \(\vek F\) and \(\vek M_{\mathrm{O}}\) point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand (KREYSZIG §9.3, Example 3, PDF p. 397), when \(\vek M_{\mathrm{O}}\) is not the zero vector. That the rule holds for any two vectors whose vector product is not zero is proved in section 2.10.1.

Let us test the definition on the door, seen from above (figure 2.106). We put the origin \(O\) at the hinge, the axis \(x\) along the door, the axis \(y\) horizontal and perpendicular to the door, and the axis \(z\) vertically up, toward the viewer. This system is right-handed. Let the door be 80 cm wide, and let the handle be right at its free end, at the point \(A = (80, 0, 0)\) cm. We measure lengths in centimetres so that the components are whole numbers, and the moment therefore in N cm, \(1\) N cm \(= 0{,}01\) N m. We push the door at the handle, perpendicular to it, with the force \(\vek F = (0, 10, 0)\) N. By (2.39)

\[\begin{aligned} \vek M_{\mathrm{O}} &= (80, 0, 0)\times(0, 10, 0) \\ &= (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 10,\ \ 0 \cdot 0 - 80 \cdot 0,\ \ 80 \cdot 10 - 0 \cdot 0) = (0, 0, 800)\ \text{N cm} . \end{aligned}\]

The moment points vertically up, along the axis of the hinge, and its size is \(800\) N cm \(= 8\) N m. From the tip of the axis \(z\), that is, from above, we see the door turn from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), counterclockwise. The same force acting 5 cm from the hinge, at the point \((5, 0, 0)\) cm, gives the moment \((5, 0, 0)\times(0, 10, 0) = (0, 0, 50)\) N cm, sixteen times smaller. A force that pulls the door along itself toward the hinge, \(\vek F = (-10, 0, 0)\) N, gives \((80, 0, 0)\times(-10, 0, 0) = \vek 0\) and does not turn the door at all.

What if the force is not perpendicular to the door? We push it at the handle with the force \(\vek F = (-6, 8, 0)\) N. It has the same size \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\) N, but points obliquely, partly toward the hinge. Then

\[\begin{aligned} \vek M_{\mathrm{O}} &= (80, 0, 0)\times(-6, 8, 0) \\ &= (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 8,\ \ 0 \cdot (-6) - 80 \cdot 0,\ \ 80 \cdot 8 - 0 \cdot (-6)) = (0, 0, 640)\ \text{N cm} , \end{aligned}\]

less than for the perpendicular force. What matters is not the distance from \(O\) to the point \(A\) but the distance from \(O\) to the line on which the force lies. The line through the point \(A\) in the direction of the force is called the line of action (premica delovanja) of the force. If \(\vek e = \vek F/|\vek F|\) is the unit vector in the direction of the force, its points are \(A + t\,\vek e\), where \(t\) is any number. The smallest distance from the point \(O\) to the points of the line of action is called the lever arm (ročica) of the force about \(O\) (CM (2.2.9), PDF p. 42, KREYSZIG §9.3, Example 3, PDF p. 397). Lemma 2.38, which follows, says that this smallest distance exists, how large it is and how it is related to the moment.

Lemma 2.38 Lever arm and the magnitude of the moment (ročica in velikost momenta)

Let a force \(\vek F \neq \vek 0\) act at a point \(A\), let \(\vek e = \vek F/|\vek F|\) be the unit vector in its direction, \(O\) a point and \(\vek r = \overrightarrow{OA}\). Then:

  1. Among the distances from \(O\) to the points \(A + t\,\vek e\) of the line of action there is a smallest one, the lever arm,
    \[\ell = \sqrt{|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2} , \tag{2.44}\]
    attained at \(t = -\vek r\cdot\vek e\).
  2. The size of the moment is the size of the force times the lever arm, \(|\vek r\times\vek F| = |\vek F|\,\ell\).
  3. If we move the force along its line of action to the point \(A' = A + t\,\vek e\), its moment about \(O\) does not change: \(\overrightarrow{OA'}\times\vek F = \vek r\times\vek F\).
Proof

We must show three statements. Throughout we use that \(\vek e\) is a unit vector, so \(\vek e\cdot\vek e = |\vek e|^2 = 1\) by item 4 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12).

1. The smallest distance.

  1. The vector from \(O\) to the point \(A + t\,\vek e\) is \(\vek r + t\,\vek e\), since the components of the vector from \(O\) to \(A\) and of the vector \(t\,\vek e\) add up to the differences of coordinates ((1.8)).
  2. By the formula for the square of the length of a sum (lemma 2.9) and by items 3 and 4 of the properties of the scalar product, the square of the distance is
    \[|\vek r + t\,\vek e|^2 = |\vek r|^2 + 2t\,(\vek r\cdot\vek e) + t^2 .\]
  3. The square \((t + \vek r\cdot\vek e)^2 = t^2 + 2t\,(\vek r\cdot\vek e) + (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2\) differs from the right side only in its last term, so
    \[|\vek r + t\,\vek e|^2 = (t + \vek r\cdot\vek e)^2 + |\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2 .\]
  4. The first term is never negative and is zero exactly at \(t = -\vek r\cdot\vek e\), at the point \(N\) where the segment from \(O\) meets the line at a right angle. The square of the distance is therefore smallest at this \(t\), and there it equals \(|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2\).
  5. Distances are nonnegative numbers, so by lemma 1.29 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, the smallest square belongs to the smallest distance. This is \(\ell = \sqrt{|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2}\).

2. The size of the moment.

  1. By lemma 1.19 on the unit vector in the direction of a vector, \(\vek F = |\vek F|\,\vek e\).
  2. By item 5 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product, \(|\vek r\times\vek F|^2 = |\vek r|^2\,|\vek F|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek F)^2\).
  3. By item 3 of the properties of the scalar product, \(\vek r\cdot\vek F = |\vek F|\,(\vek r\cdot\vek e)\), so \(|\vek r\times\vek F|^2 = |\vek F|^2\,\big(|\vek r|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek e)^2\big) = |\vek F|^2\,\ell^2\).
  4. The numbers \(|\vek r\times\vek F|\) and \(|\vek F|\,\ell\) are nonnegative and have the same square, so by lemma 1.29 they are equal.

3. Moving along the line.

  1. By step 1 of part 1 the vector from \(O\) to \(A' = A + t\,\vek e\) is \(\vek r + t\,\vek e\).
  2. By items 2 and 3 of the lemma on the properties of the vector product, \((\vek r + t\,\vek e)\times\vek F = \vek r\times\vek F + t\,(\vek e\times\vek F)\).
  3. Since \(\vek F = |\vek F|\,\vek e\), items 3 and 1 of the same lemma give \(\vek e\times\vek F = |\vek F|\,(\vek e\times\vek e) = \vek 0\). What remains is \(\vek r\times\vek F\).

Source: CM (2.2.9), (2.2.10) (PDF p. 42), KREYSZIG §9.3, Example 3 (PDF p. 397). The sources write the size of the moment with the lever arm and with the angle between \(\vek r\) and \(\vek F\). The proof through the smallest distance is not from the sources.

The lemma says that the moment does not depend on where on its line of action the force acts, only on the line itself and on the force. Its size is the force times the lever arm, which is the formula with which CM and KREYSZIG introduce the moment. Let us check this on the oblique force \(\vek F = (-6, 8, 0)\) N on the door. The unit vector in its direction is \(\vek e = (-\tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0)\), and \(\vek r\cdot\vek e = 80 \cdot (-\tfrac35) = -48\) cm. By (2.44) the lever arm is

\[\ell = \sqrt{80^2 - 48^2}\ \text{cm} = \sqrt{6400 - 2304}\ \text{cm} = \sqrt{4096}\ \text{cm} = 64\ \text{cm} .\]

By item 1 the nearest point \(N\) of the line of action lies at \(t = 48\) cm, that is, 48 cm from \(A\) in the direction of the force (figure 2.106). The segment \(ON\) meets the line at a right angle. By item 2 the size of the moment is \(10\ \text{N} \cdot 64\ \text{cm} = 640\) N cm, exactly the component \(z\) we computed above. The oblique force turns the door less strongly because its lever arm is 64 cm, shorter than 80 cm. For a force acting along the door toward the hinge, the line of action passes through \(O\), the lever arm is zero, and so is the moment.

2.8.3 The second condition of equilibrium

Now we can write as an equation what it means that the forces do not tend to turn a body. Let forces \(\vek F_1, \vek F_2, \dots, \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) act on a body at points \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) (two of them for the ruler below), and let \(O\) be a chosen point. The forces do not tend to turn the body when the sum of their moments about \(O\) is the zero vector:

\[\vek r_1\times\vek F_1 + \vek r_2\times\vek F_2 + \dots + \vek r_{\mathrm{k}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0 , \tag{2.45}\]

where \(\vek r_1 = \overrightarrow{OA_1}\) is the vector from \(O\) to the point at which the force \(\vek F_1\) acts, and the same for the other forces. This is the second condition of equilibrium of definition 2.3, written with numbers (SADD §3.7, (3.7.6), PDF pp. 77-78, EP §2.2.2, p. 54). When a force is distributed over a part of the surface or over all the material, like the weight, we picture it by section 2.1 as the sum of many small forces, one on each bit, and its moment as the sum of their moments. This is a simplification, and the exact summation we will meet in chapter 4. Equation (2.45) is a vector equation, so it means three equations for numbers, one for each component.

Where does this condition come from? Like the condition for the forces, it is a law of mechanics that we do not derive from others. CM writes it for every part of a body, also for a body that moves (figure 2.107): the sum of the moments of all forces on a part of a body equals the rate at which the sum of the moments of the momenta (gibalne količine) of its bits changes, the momentum of a bit being its mass times its velocity. CM calls it the principle of balance of angular momentum (načelo o vrtilni količini) (CM §5.3.3, (5.3.28), PDF pp. 232-233). For a body at rest all velocities are zero, the right side is zero, and (2.45) remains. We cannot get it from the condition for the forces, as the ruler shows.

Let the ruler in figure 2.7 be 30 cm long. We put the origin \(O\) at its centre, the axis \(x\) along the ruler, the axis \(y\) horizontally across it and the axis \(z\) vertically up (figure 2.108). The ends are \(A_1 = (15, 0, 0)\) cm and \(A_2 = (-15, 0, 0)\) cm. The vectors from \(O\) to the ends are \(\vek r_1 = (15, 0, 0)\) cm and \(\vek r_2 = (-15, 0, 0)\) cm. The force \(\vek F = (0, 5, 0)\) N acts on the right end, the force \(-\vek F\) on the left end. The resultant is zero, and the first condition of equilibrium holds. The moments about \(O\), however, are

\[(15, 0, 0)\times(0, 5, 0) = (0, 0, 75)\ \text{N cm} , \qquad (-15, 0, 0)\times(0, -5, 0) = (0, 0, 75)\ \text{N cm} .\]

Their sum \((0, 0, 150)\) N cm is not the zero vector, and the second condition does not hold. The moment points vertically up. From the tip of the axis \(z\), from above, we see the ruler turn from the axis \(x\) toward the axis \(y\), counterclockwise, as the grey arrow in figure 2.7 shows. The forces along the ruler, \((5, 0, 0)\) N at the right end and \((-5, 0, 0)\) N at the left end, have the moments

\[(15, 0, 0)\times(5, 0, 0) = \vek 0 , \qquad (-15, 0, 0)\times(-5, 0, 0) = \vek 0 ,\]

because the vector to the point of action points in the direction of the force or opposite to it. The line of action therefore passes through \(O\), and the lever arm is zero (lemma 2.38 on the lever arm and the magnitude of the moment). Such forces do not turn the ruler. In section 2.1 we claimed this for bars pulled along their axis, and now it is proved.

About which point \(O\) should we compute the moments? For the ruler, let us choose the left end \(A_2\) instead of the centre. The vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_1\) is \((30, 0, 0)\) cm, the lengths of \(\vek r_2\) and \(\vek r_1\) together, and the vector from \(A_2\) to \(A_2\) is the zero vector, so the sum of the moments is

\[(30, 0, 0)\times(0, 5, 0) + \vek 0\times(0, -5, 0) = (0, 0, 150)\ \text{N cm} ,\]

the same as about the centre. This is no coincidence.

Lemma 2.39 The moment does not depend on the point (moment ni odvisen od točke)

Let forces \(\vek F_1, \vek F_2, \dots, \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) act at points \(A_1\), \(A_2, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\), and let their resultant be the zero vector, \(\vek F_1 + \vek F_2 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\). Then for any two points \(O\) and \(Q\)

\[\overrightarrow{QA_1}\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \overrightarrow{QA_{\mathrm{k}}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \overrightarrow{OA_1}\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \overrightarrow{OA_{\mathrm{k}}}\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} .\]
Proof

We write each vector from \(Q\) to one of the points \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{k}}\) as a path through the point \(O\) and use the splitting of a sum.

  1. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{QO}\). By (1.8), \(\overrightarrow{QA_1} = \vek d + \overrightarrow{OA_1}\), since for example \(x_{\mathrm{A}_1} - x_{\mathrm{Q}} = (x_{\mathrm{O}} - x_{\mathrm{Q}}) + (x_{\mathrm{A}_1} - x_{\mathrm{O}})\), and the same for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The same holds for the other points.
  2. By item 2 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product, for the force \(\vek F_1\) at the point \(A_1\) \(\overrightarrow{QA_1}\times\vek F_1 = \vek d\times\vek F_1 + \overrightarrow{OA_1}\times\vek F_1\), and the same for the other forces.
  3. We add all \(k\) equalities. The terms with \(\vek d\) give, by the same item 2 applied to the second factor, \(\vek d\times\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek d\times\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek d\times(\vek F_1 + \dots + \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}) = \vek d\times\vek 0\).
  4. By item 3 of the same lemma, applied with the number zero, \(\vek d\times\vek 0 = \vek d\times(0\,\vek d) = 0\,(\vek d\times\vek d) = \vek 0\). What remains is the sum of the moments about \(O\).

Source: SADD §3.7 (PDF p. 78) says that the point about which the moments are computed can be chosen arbitrarily. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

So when the resultant of the forces is zero, the second condition of equilibrium does not depend on the choice of the point \(O\). If the sum of the moments is zero about one point, it is zero about every point. We can therefore choose the point that makes the computation shortest, for example one through which as many lines of action as possible pass, since forces on these lines have no moment. For the ruler the lemma says that the pair of forces \(\vek F\) and \(-\vek F\) turns it with the moment \((0, 0, 150)\) N cm no matter about which point we compute it.

2.8.4 Moments on a small cube

We now apply the second condition of equilibrium to the same small cube to which we applied the first condition in section 2.7. Let the body be in equilibrium and \(P\) a point in its interior. We put the origin of a right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system at \(P\). In thought we cut out of the body the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and edges parallel to the axes. Its faces lie in the planes \(x = \pm h/2\), \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\). The cube is a part of a body in equilibrium, so it is in equilibrium itself (section 2.1), and by (2.45) the sum of the moments of all forces on it about \(P\) is the zero vector. Two kinds of forces act on the cube. The rest of the body acts on it across its six faces, and the body force (definition 2.28), for example the weight, acts on all its material. Its density \(\vek b\) is the force per unit volume.

We know the force across a face from the stress components. As in section 2.7 we write the point with the traction vector, \(\vek t(Q, \vek n)\), because we compare traction vectors at different points. On the face \(x = h/2\) the outward normal of the cube is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and at a point \(Q\) of this face the traction vector \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(Q), \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q), \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(Q)\big)\) acts per unit area (definition 2.27). On the opposite face \(x = -h/2\) the outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut the traction at its point \(Q\) is \(\vek t(Q, -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = -\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). The same holds on the other four faces. The stress components change from point to point, so the force is not necessarily distributed evenly over a face.

We treat a distributed force as in sections 2.1 and 2.7, as the sum of many small forces on small patches. We divide a face of the cube by lines parallel to its sides into equal small rectangles. On a rectangle with the area \(\Delta A\) and the centre \(Q\) the force \(\vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\) acts at \(Q\), where \(\vek t(Q)\) is the force per unit area at \(Q\), on the face \(x = h/2\) therefore \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). The moment of the distributed force is the sum of the moments of these small forces. In the same way we divide the volume of the cube into equal small cubes. This is a simplification, and in section 2.7 we took the same summation as an assumption about the forces on the faces of the cube. SADD and CM write the moment of a distributed force exactly, by exact adding up over a surface and over a body (SADD (3.7.6), PDF p. 78, CM (5.3.28), PDF p. 233), which we will meet in chapter 4. Until then we compute with sums. We need two facts about them, collected in lemma 2.40.

Lemma 2.40 Moment of a distributed force (moment porazdeljene sile)

Let a force act on a flat face with the area \(A\), equal per unit area to \(\vek t(Q)\) at the point \(Q\). We divide the face into small bits. On a bit with the area \(\Delta A\) the force \(\vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\) acts at a chosen point \(Q\) of the bit, and the moment of the distributed force about a point \(O\) is the sum of the moments of these forces. Then:

  1. If the face is a rectangle with the centre \(S\), divided by lines parallel to its sides into equal rectangles, the points \(Q\) are their centres, and the force is distributed evenly, \(\vek t(Q) = \vek t_0\) for all \(Q\), then its moment about \(O\) equals \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times(A\,\vek t_0)\), the moment of the resultant \(A\,\vek t_0\) acting at the centre \(S\).
  2. If \(|\vek t(Q)| \le c\) for all chosen points \(Q\) and every point of the face is at most \(r_{\max}\) away from \(O\), then every component of the moment is at most \(c\,A\,r_{\max}\) in absolute value.

Item 2 holds in the same way for a force distributed over a volume \(V\), equal per unit volume to \(\vek b(Q)\), with \(|\vek b(Q)| \le c\) at all chosen points \(Q\) of the bits of volume. Every component of its moment is then at most \(c\,V\,r_{\max}\).

Proof

We show both statements on the sum of the moments of the small forces.

1. An evenly distributed force.

  1. Lines parallel to the sides divide each side into equal parts, so the division is the same on both sides of the centre \(S\). A rectangle whose centre is moved from \(S\) by a vector \(\vek s\) has a partner whose centre is moved from \(S\) by \(-\vek s\). When the number of rectangles is odd in both directions, the middle rectangle has its centre at \(S\) and is its own partner.
  2. All rectangles have the same area \(\Delta A\), so the same force \(\vek f = \vek t_0\,\Delta A\) acts on each. The vectors from \(O\) to the centres of a pair are \(\overrightarrow{OS} + \vek s\) and \(\overrightarrow{OS} - \vek s\).
  3. By items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product, the sum of the moments of the pair is
    \[(\overrightarrow{OS} + \vek s)\times\vek f + (\overrightarrow{OS} - \vek s)\times\vek f = 2\,\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f + \vek s\times\vek f - \vek s\times\vek f = 2\,\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f .\]
    The middle rectangle, if there is one, has the moment \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f\).
  4. Each rectangle therefore contributes \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times\vek f\) to the sum, as if its force acted at \(S\). By item 2 of the same lemma the sum is \(\overrightarrow{OS}\times(\vek f + \vek f + \dots + \vek f)\). The sum of the forces is \(\vek t_0\) times the sum of the areas, that is, \(A\,\vek t_0\).

2. A bound for the moment.

  1. Take one bit of the division with the chosen point \(Q\) and the force \(\vek f = \vek t(Q)\,\Delta A\), and let \(\vek r = \overrightarrow{OQ}\). By item 5 of the lemma on the properties of the vector product, \(|\vek r\times\vek f|^2 = |\vek r|^2\,|\vek f|^2 - (\vek r\cdot\vek f)^2 \le |\vek r|^2\,|\vek f|^2\), so by lemma 1.29 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|\vek r\times\vek f| \le |\vek r|\,|\vek f|\).
  2. We have \(|\vek r| \le r_{\max}\), and by (1.10) \(|\vek f| = |\vek t(Q)|\,\Delta A \le c\,\Delta A\), because \(\Delta A\) is a positive number. Therefore \(|\vek r\times\vek f| \le c\,r_{\max}\,\Delta A\).
  3. Every component of a vector is at most its length in absolute value, since for example \(q_{\mathrm{x}}^2 \le q_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + q_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + q_{\mathrm{z}}^2\), as in step 3 of the proof of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26). In the figure the axes and the edges of the box are the components.
  4. A component of the moment of the distributed force is the sum of the same components of the moments of all bits. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) its absolute value is at most the sum of the absolute values, and by steps 2 and 3 this is at most \(c\,r_{\max}\) times the sum of the areas, that is, \(c\,A\,r_{\max}\). In the figure the two sums are on two number lines, and the dashed guide marks the upper sum \(2{,}2\), which is smaller than the lower \(4{,}8\).
  5. For a force distributed over a volume we repeat steps 1 to 4 with bits of volume \(\Delta V\) and forces \(\vek b(Q)\,\Delta V\).

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

Item 1 says that an evenly distributed force turns a body as if all of it acted at the centre of the face (figure 2.114). The reason is symmetry. Every bit on one side of the centre has a partner on the other side, and the contributions of the vectors \(\vek s\) and \(-\vek s\) cancel in the sum of the moments. In section 2.7 we used the same idea of pairs of patches symmetric about the centre for the force across a face. Item 2 says that a small force per unit area on a small face near \(O\) gives a small moment.

First let us compute what the moment would be if the stress components at all points of the cube were the same as at \(P\). On the face \(x = h/2\) an evenly distributed force with the traction \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) per unit area would then act. The face is a square with the area \(h^2\) and the centre \((h/2, 0, 0)\), so by item 1 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force and by (2.39) its moment about \(P\) is

\[\Big(\frac h2, 0, 0\Big)\times h^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = \frac{h^3}{2}\,(0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) .\]

On the opposite face \(x = -h/2\) both factors are opposite, the vector to the centre \((-h/2, 0, 0)\) and the force \(-h^2\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\). By item 3 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product the signs cancel, \((-1)(-1) = 1\), and the moment is the same. We compute the other faces in the same way:

faces moment of each of the two faces
\(x = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\)
\(y = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ 0,\ -\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\)
\(z = \pm h/2\) \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(-\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}},\ 0)\)

We count each row twice, once for each face, so the sum of all six moments is

\[h^3\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\big) . \tag{2.46}\]

The normal components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) do not appear in the sum. Their forces point along the axis on which the centre of the face lies, so the line of action passes through \(P\), the lever arm is zero, and so is the moment (figure 2.115, right). Only the shear components appear. Let us look at the component \(z\). In the figure the axis \(x\) points right, the axis \(y\) up and the axis \(z\) toward the viewer. The forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2\) on the faces \(x = \pm h/2\) point in opposite directions on opposite sides of \(P\), each with the lever arm \(h/2\), and turn the cube about the axis \(z\) counterclockwise. The forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}h^2\) on the faces \(y = \pm h/2\) turn it clockwise (figure 2.115, left and middle). The component \(z\) of the sum is zero only if the two pairs are equally strong, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

Let us read the same balance straight from figure 2.115, without the vector product. Only four shear forces turn the cube about the axis \(z\) through \(P\). By lemma 2.38 on the lever arm and the magnitude of the moment, the magnitude of the moment of each is the force times the lever arm. We count counterclockwise turning as positive and clockwise turning as negative, as in the component \(z\) of the vector (2.46):

\[\underbrace{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2 \cdot \frac h2}_{\text{face } \mathrm{x} = \mathrm{h}/2} + \underbrace{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2 \cdot \frac h2}_{\text{face } \mathrm{x} = -\mathrm{h}/2} - \underbrace{\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}h^2 \cdot \frac h2}_{\text{face } \mathrm{y} = \mathrm{h}/2} - \underbrace{\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}h^2 \cdot \frac h2}_{\text{face } \mathrm{y} = -\mathrm{h}/2} = 0 . \tag{2.47}\]

The first two terms are the forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2\) on the right and the left face, each with the lever arm \(h/2\). The other two are the forces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}h^2\) on the top and the bottom face, again with the lever arm \(h/2\). Each term is \(\tfrac12 h^3\) times one stress component. We divide the equation by \(\tfrac12 h^3\) and are left with \(2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0\), that is, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). This is the component \(z\) of the vector (2.46), written term by term. Every part of the equation has its own why, and we show each in the figure:

  1. Why must the sum be zero? The cube is a part of a body at rest, so it does not start to turn. This is what the second condition of equilibrium (2.45) demands: what turns the cube one way must equal what turns it the other way, as with the lever in section 2.8.2.
  2. Why is the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2\)? Stress is force per unit area, and the face of the cube next to which the force is drawn has the area \(h \cdot h = h^2\).
  3. Why is the lever arm \(h/2\)? The force lies in the face, and the face is half a side away from \(P\).
  4. Why do the forces on opposite faces have the same sign? On the opposite face the force is reversed (lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut), but so is the side on which the face lies. Both forces therefore turn the same way and form a pair.
  5. Must the piece be a cube? No. In a cuboid with the sides \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) along the axes \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), the face perpendicular to the axis \(x\) has the area \(b\,c\) and the lever arm \(a/2\), and the face perpendicular to the axis \(y\) has the area \(a\,c\) and the lever arm \(b/2\). Each of the four terms is therefore \(\tfrac12\,a\,b\,c\) times a stress component, and the common factor, half the volume, cancels again.

In the lectures equation (2.47) is written for just such a cuboid, with the sides \(l_1\), \(l_2\), \(l_3\) and the axes \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), and with the values of the stress at the centres of the faces, which approach the value at the point as the cuboid gets smaller. We have replaced them by the values at \(P\) already here. How much we neglected by that is what we ask now.

What about everything we left out? The moments in (2.46) are proportional to \(h^3\): the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}h^2\) is proportional to the area of the face \(h^2\) and the lever arm to half the side \(h/2\). The weight of the cube is proportional to its volume \(h^3\), and every bit of the cube is at most as far from \(P\) as a corner, three half sides \(h/2\) give \(\sqrt{3\,(h/2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) (figure 2.116). By item 2 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force the moment of the weight is therefore at most proportional to \(h^4\). The stress components also change across the cube. For a continuously differentiable field the difference between the value at a point of a face and the value at \(P\) is at most proportional to the distance, that is, to \(h\), which we will show in the proof below. The force due to this difference is therefore at most proportional to \(h \cdot h^2\), and its moment at most to \(h \cdot h^2 \cdot h = h^4\), with the size of the cube, the area and the lever arm. When we shrink the cube, \(h^4\) decreases faster than \(h^3\).

How much faster, let us show on a steel cube with \(\rho g = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 = 76\,518\) N/m³, as for the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2. In it the density of the weight is the same everywhere in the cube, so the moment of the weight about the centre \(P\) is in fact exactly zero, for the same reason as in item 1 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force: two small cubes symmetric about \(P\) carry equal forces, and their vectors from \(P\) are \(\vek s\) and \(-\vek s\), as for the pieces of the face in figure 2.114, so their moments cancel. We need the bound of item 2 for a body force whose density varies across the cube, and the table shows how fast such a bound shrinks when the density is at most \(\rho g\) in size. Suppose \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) were larger than \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) by 1 MPa. By (2.46) the moment of the pairs would be \(h^3 \cdot 1\) MPa, and the bound for the moment of the body force, by the same item 2, the force \(\rho g\,h^3\) times the largest distance \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\). We computed with NumPy:

\(h\) \(h^3 \cdot 1\) MPa \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\rho g\,h^4\) ratio
1 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-3}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-8}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-5}\)
0,1 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-6}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-12}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
0,01 mm \(1 \cdot 10^{-9}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-16}\) N m \(6{,}627 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

When we decrease \(h\) by a factor of 10, the moment of the pairs decreases by a factor of 1000, the bound for the moment of the body force by a factor of 10 000, and their ratio falls by a factor of 10 (figure 2.117, the horizontal axis is \(h\), the vertical one the moment). In a small enough cube the body force cannot balance any difference between \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) other than zero. The same holds for the change of stress across the cube.
