In the hanging bar the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) changes over the distance \(h\) by \(\rho g\,h\), for \(h = 1\) mm by \(76{,}52\) Pa, and the moment that such a change gives is again at most proportional to \(h^4\). The only possibility left is that the differences in (2.46) are zero. This is the heart of the derivation, which we now write down precisely. As with the tetrahedron, two quantities shrink together, but at different rates, and their ratio decides.

2.8.5 Symmetry of stress

We state the theorem with assumptions similar to those of section 2.7 but somewhat stronger: there we required the derivatives only at the point \(P\), here we require them near it, and boundedness of the body force density was not needed there. The first is that the stress components are continuously differentiable fields (definition 1.91). We will need only what theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step uses of it, and we write that into the theorem. The second concerns the body force. Its density is to be bounded near \(P\). This holds for the weight, whose density has the size \(\rho g\), when the density of the material \(\rho\) is bounded near \(P\), for example equal everywhere. It holds also for every body force density that is continuous at \(P\), since then near \(P\) each of its components differs from its value at \(P\) by less than 1 N/m³ (definition 1.68 with the error 1 N/m³). In the proof this bound gives, in step 10, the term \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B\,h^4\), which shrinks faster than the moment of the pairs. The third assumption is the way we compute the moments of distributed forces.

Figure 2.118 shows what we need near the point \(P\). On the left is the point \(P\) and around it the ball with the radius \(\delta_1\), in which we will bound the difference of stress, smaller than both earlier balls. In it lies a small cube with the edge \(h\), whose corner is \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) from \(P\), and a point \(Q\) with the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\). We explain the right graph with its axes in steps 2 and 3 of the proof.

Theorem 2.41 Symmetry of stress (simetrija napetosti)

Let a body be in equilibrium, \(P\) a point in its interior and \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) the axes of a right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. Assume:

  1. every stress component is defined at all points that are less than some number \(r_1 > 0\) away from \(P\), has all three partial derivatives there, and these are continuous at \(P\),
  2. there are numbers \(B\) and \(r_0 > 0\) such that the body force density \(\vek b\) has a size of at most \(B\) at every point less than \(r_0\) away from \(P\),
  3. only forces across its surface and the body force act on any part of the body, and their moments are computed as sums of the moments of small forces, as in lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force, where a face that is a rectangle is divided by lines parallel to its sides into equal rectangles with the points at their centres.

Then at the point \(P\) for pairs of shear components

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} . \tag{2.48}\]
Proof

We must show that the differences \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) at \(P\) are zero. We write the equilibrium of moments of a small cube with the centre \(P\). The moment given by the values of stress at \(P\) is proportional to \(h^3\), everything else at most proportional to \(h^4\).

  1. We put the origin at \(P\). For \(h > 0\) we take the cube with centre \(P\), side \(h\) and faces in the planes \(x = \pm h/2\), \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\). Every point of the cube has coordinates that are at most \(h/2\) in absolute value, so by (1.10) it is at most \(\sqrt{3\,(h/2)^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) away from \(P\).
  2. We apply theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step to the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with the error \(\eta_1 = 1\) Pa/m. Its hypotheses are assumption 1. So there is \(\delta_{\mathrm{xy}} > 0\) such that for every point \(Q\) with the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) and \(0 < |\overrightarrow{PQ}| < \delta_{\mathrm{xy}}\)
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) = \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x}\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y}\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z}\,\Delta z + R , \qquad |R| \le \eta_1\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}| ,\]
    with the partial derivatives at \(P\). The first three terms are the line in the right graph, and \(R\) lies in the band of width \(\eta_1\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) around it.
  3. Each of the components \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z\) is at most \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers therefore the difference lies in the cone of width \(G_{\mathrm{xy}}\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\), namely
    \[|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(Q) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}(P)| \le G_{\mathrm{xy}}\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}| , \qquad G_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x}\Big| + \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y}\Big| + \Big|\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z}\Big| + \eta_1 .\]
    At \(Q = P\) the inequality holds because both sides are zero.
  4. We do the same for all nine stress components. Let \(G\) be the largest of the nine numbers \(G_{\mathrm{xx}}, G_{\mathrm{xy}}, \dots, G_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(\delta_1\) the smallest of the nine numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{xx}}, \delta_{\mathrm{xy}}, \dots, \delta_{\mathrm{zz}}\). For every point \(Q\) with \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}| < \delta_1\) each stress component at \(Q\) then differs from its value at \(P\) by at most \(G\,|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\).
  5. Since \(P\) is in the interior of the body, we can choose \(h\) so small that the whole cube lies in the body and that \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) is smaller than \(\delta_1\) and than \(r_0\). By step 1 the bound of step 4 and assumption 2 then hold at every point of the cube.
  6. The cube is a part of a body in equilibrium, so it is in equilibrium itself (section 2.1), and by (2.45) the sum of the moments of all forces on it about \(P\) is the zero vector. By assumption 3 these are the forces across the six faces and the body force.
  7. On the face \(x = h/2\) (with axes \(y\) and \(z\)) the outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the force per unit area at its point \(Q\) is the traction vector \(\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) (definition 2.27). On the right, the vector starts at the origin \(O\). We write it as the sum \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}}\) \(+\) \(\vek q(Q)\), where \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) with the values at \(P\), and \(\vek q(Q)\) is the difference. By steps 4 and 5 each component of the difference is at most \(G\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\) in absolute value, so by (1.10) \(|\vek q(Q)| \le \sqrt3 \cdot G\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h = \tfrac32\,G\,h\).
  8. The force on each rectangle of the division of the face is the sum of the forces \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}}\,\Delta A\) and \(\vek q(Q)\,\Delta A\), so by item 2 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product the moment of the force on the face is the sum of two moments. The first is the moment of the evenly distributed force \(\vek t_{\mathrm{P}}\), and by item 1 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force it equals \(\tfrac{h^3}{2}\,(0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\), as in the table before the theorem. The second is the moment of the force \(\vek q\). By item 2 of the same lemma with \(c = \tfrac32\,G\,h\), \(A = h^2\) and \(r_{\max} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\), each of its components is at most \(\tfrac32\,G\,h \cdot h^2 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h = \tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4\) in absolute value.
  9. We proceed in the same way on the other five faces. On the face \(x = -h/2\) the force per unit area is, by lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, \(-\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\), like the opposite forces in the figure, and on the faces \(y = \pm h/2\) and \(z = \pm h/2\) it is \(\pm\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\pm\vek t(Q, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\). The moments of the even parts are in the table before the theorem, and their sum is (2.46). The moments of the differences are again at most \(\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4\) in each component.
  10. By step 5 the body force density has a size of at most \(B\) at every point of the cube. By item 2 of the lemma on the moment of a distributed force for the volume \(V = h^3\) and \(r_{\max} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,h\), each component of its moment is at most \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B\,h^4\) in absolute value.
  11. The component \(z\) of the sum of all moments is zero. It consists of the component \(z\) of the vector (2.46), \(h^3\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\), the moment of both pairs of shear forces, the six components of the moments of the differences from steps 8 and 9, and the component of the moment of the body force from step 10. So \(h^3\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\) is the negative of the sum of the other seven numbers, and by the triangle inequality for numbers
    \[h^3\,|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le 6 \cdot \frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,G\,h^4 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B\,h^4 = K\,h^4 , \qquad K = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\,G + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B .\]
  12. We divide the inequality by the positive number \(h^3\) and get \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le K\,h\). This holds for every \(h > 0\) that satisfies step 5. On the axes of the graph \(h\) is horizontal and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}|\) vertical.
  13. We choose any number \(\eta > 0\). We choose \(h\) so that it satisfies step 5 and \(K\,h \le \eta\). For \(K > 0\) it is enough to require also \(h \le \eta/K\), for \(K = 0\) every \(h\) of step 5 will do. Then \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}| \le \eta\).
  14. So the nonnegative number \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}|\) is not larger than any positive number \(\eta\). By lemma 1.35 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers it is zero, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\).
  15. The components \(x\) and \(y\) of the sum of the moments give, by the same steps, \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}| \le K\,h\) and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}| \le K\,h\), so also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

Source: SADD (3.7.7) (PDF p. 79), CM (5.3.31) (PDF p. 234), EP (2.2.17) (p. 54), BOWER §2.3.2 (PDF p. 78). SADD, CM and BOWER derive the theorem from the equilibrium of moments on a finite part of the body with integrals, EP with moments on a small box, much as we do. The proof with bounds is not from the sources.

Next to Cauchy's formula, this is the second result on which the whole theory of stress rests, so let us remember it. The proof showed why it holds. The shear forces on opposite faces of a small cube form pairs that turn the cube, and the moment of each pair is proportional to the area of the face and to the lever arm, that is, to \(h^3\). Everything else, the body force and the change of stress across the cube, gives moments at most proportional to \(h^4\), which therefore shrink faster. In a small cube the pairs of shear forces must therefore balance each other. The idea is the same as with the tetrahedron in section 2.6.2, where the weight disappeared because it shrank faster than the forces across the faces.

What does the theorem mean for the material? A shear component never appears alone. When a shear component in the direction of the axis \(y\) acts on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), an equally large shear component in the direction of the axis \(x\) acts on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) through the same point. In figure 2.115 the forces on the left and in the middle must therefore be equally large, and the counterclockwise and the clockwise turning cancel, so the cube does not turn.

Where does the theorem fail? Assumption 3 excludes bodies on which, besides forces, distributed moments act that are not moments of forces. CM and EP call them body couples (telesni momenti) and say that without them the second condition of equilibrium gives the symmetry of stress (CM §5.3.3, PDF pp. 232-234, EP §2.2.2, p. 54). For materials whose inner structure carries such moments too, CM writes additional equations (CM §5.3.3.2, PDF pp. 234-235). We do not treat such materials in this book. Assumption 1 excludes points at which the stress changes by a jump. The theorem does not cover them, but the symmetry holds at every point on both sides of the jump. We proved the theorem for a body in equilibrium. It also holds for a body that moves and accelerates. In motion the sum of the moments of the forces on the cube is no longer the zero vector. By the principle of balance of angular momentum from section 2.8.3 it equals the rate at which the sum of the moments of the momenta of the bits of the cube changes, and this rate is the sum of the moments of the masses of the bits times their accelerations (CM (5.3.28), PDF p. 233, with the right side rearranged on p. 234, all by exact summation over the volume). This sum is the moment of a distributed force with the density \(\rho\,\vek a\) per unit volume, where \(\rho\) is the density of the material and \(\vek a\) the acceleration of the bit. If its size near \(P\) is at most \(B_{\mathrm{a}}\), then by item 2 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force every component of this sum is at most \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B_{\mathrm{a}}\,h^4\), just as for the weight in step 10 of the proof. In step 11 the number \(K\) therefore grows by \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,B_{\mathrm{a}}\), and steps 12 to 15 stay as they are. How much is that? Let a steel cube with the side \(h = 1\) mm have the acceleration 1000 m/s², about a hundred times the gravitational one. Then \(\rho\,|\vek a| = 7800 \cdot 1000 = 7{,}8 \cdot 10^6\) N/m³ and the bound is \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \cdot 7{,}8 \cdot 10^6 \cdot (10^{-3})^4 = 6{,}755 \cdot 10^{-6}\) N m, less than a hundredth of the moment of the pairs \(10^{-3}\) N m at the difference of 1 MPa from the table in section 2.8.4. For a cube ten times smaller the share is ten times smaller again. CM arrives at the symmetry for a body in motion by exact summation (CM (5.3.30), (5.3.31), PDF p. 234). The term with the acceleration disappears in the same way as the weight, as it did for Cauchy's formula in section 2.6.4.

2.8.6 Reciprocity of traction vectors

We wrote the symmetry with components, that is, for faces perpendicular to the axes. What does it say about two arbitrary planes through the same point? It says this: as much as the first plane feels in the direction of the normal of the second, so much the second feels in the direction of the normal of the first. Let us look at the figure first and then at the lemma.

Take a point \(P\) inside the body and cut the body through it twice in thought (figure 2.121, the axis \(x\) points right, the axis \(y\) up). We draw the first cut on the left. Light grey is the part of the body we observe, and \(\vek n\) is its outward normal. The rest of the body acts on it across the cut with a force per unit area, the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\). We draw the second cut through the same point on the right, with the outward normal \(\vek m\) and the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek m)\). Now we project each of the traction vectors onto the normal of the other cut (definition 2.13). In the left picture we draw a line through \(P\) in the direction \(\vek m\) and drop a perpendicular onto it from the tip of the vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\). The blue segment from \(P\) to its foot is the part of the vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) in the direction \(\vek m\), of the length \(\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m\). In the right picture we draw a line in the direction \(\vek n\) in the same way, and the blue segment is the part of the vector \(\vek t(\vek m)\) in the direction \(\vek n\), of the length \(\vek t(\vek m)\cdot\vek n\). The cuts are different and so are the traction vectors, different in length and in direction. But the blue segments have the same length, and that for every choice of the two cuts.

Lemma 2.42 Reciprocity of traction vectors (vzajemnost vektorjev napetosti)

At a point \(P\) of a body let Cauchy's formula in the form (2.27) and the symmetry of stress (2.48) hold, with the components written in a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. Then for any two unit vectors \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\vek m = (m_{\mathrm{x}}, m_{\mathrm{y}}, m_{\mathrm{z}})\)

\[\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m = \vek t(\vek m)\cdot\vek n . \tag{2.49}\]
\[t_{\mathrm{i}}^{(\vek n)}\,m_{\mathrm{i}} = t_{\mathrm{i}}^{(\vek m)}\,n_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{2.49}\]

The projection of the traction vector on the plane with the normal \(\vek n\) onto the direction \(\vek m\) equals the projection of the traction vector on the plane with the normal \(\vek m\) onto the direction \(\vek n\).

Proof

We must show that the numbers \(\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m\) and \(\vek t(\vek m)\cdot\vek n\) are equal. We write both out in components and compare them term by term.

  1. By (2.6), \(\vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m = t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n)\,m_{\mathrm{x}} + t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n)\,m_{\mathrm{y}} + t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n)\,m_{\mathrm{z}}\), the length of the blue segment in the left picture.
  2. We insert the components of the vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) from (2.27) and multiply each bracket by a component of the vector \(\vek m\). We get nine products, which we write in three rows:
    \[\begin{aligned} \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m = {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} m_{\mathrm{x}} \\ {} + {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} m_{\mathrm{y}} \\ {} + {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} m_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]
  3. For the second segment we repeat steps 1 and 2 with the roles of the vectors \(\vek n\) and \(\vek m\) exchanged:
    \[\begin{aligned} \vek t(\vek m)\cdot\vek n = {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,m_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{x}} \\ {} + {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,m_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{y}} \\ {} + {} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,m_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. The three terms with two equal indices are the same in both sums, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), because the order of multiplying numbers does not matter.
  5. We pair the remaining six terms. By (2.48), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{x}}\) equals its partner \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\). Likewise for the other five:
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{y}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,m_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} m_{\mathrm{x}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{z}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{x}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} m_{\mathrm{y}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,m_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{z}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{y}} . \end{aligned}\]
  6. Every term of the first sum therefore equals exactly one term of the second, so the sums are equal, and the blue segments have the same length.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources. The proof uses only Cauchy's formula (2.27) and the symmetry of stress (2.48).

Let us test the lemma with numbers, on the state drawn in figure 2.121. We chose the numbers ourselves. At the point \(P\) let

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 67\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 53\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 24\ \text{MPa} ,\]

and let all components with the index \(z\) be zero. For the cuts take \(\vek n = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0)\) and \(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\). By (2.27) the components of the vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) are

\[\begin{aligned} t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} = 67 \cdot \tfrac35 + 24 \cdot \tfrac45 = 40{,}2 + 19{,}2 = 59{,}4\ \text{MPa} , \\ t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} = 24 \cdot \tfrac35 + 53 \cdot \tfrac45 = 14{,}4 + 42{,}4 = 56{,}8\ \text{MPa} , \end{aligned}\]

and the vector \(\vek t(\vek m) = \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) is, by definition 2.27, \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = (67, 24, 0)\) MPa. The two projections are

\[\begin{aligned} \vek t(\vek n)\cdot\vek m &= 59{,}4 \cdot 1 + 56{,}8 \cdot 0 = 59{,}4\ \text{MPa} , \\ \vek t(\vek m)\cdot\vek n &= 67 \cdot \tfrac35 + 24 \cdot \tfrac45 = 40{,}2 + 19{,}2 = 59{,}4\ \text{MPa} , \end{aligned}\]

the two blue segments. The two computations look the same, but the number 24 in them is not the same component. In the first it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), the shear component on the face perpendicular to the axis \(y\), which Cauchy's formula multiplies by \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\). In the second it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the component \(y\) of the vector \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\). They are equal only because of the symmetry. If we had \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 24\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 20\) MPa, the first projection would be \(67 \cdot \tfrac35 + 20 \cdot \tfrac45 = 56{,}2\) MPa and the second still \(59{,}4\) MPa, and the blue segments would differ by \(3{,}2\) MPa. Without the symmetry of stress the lemma therefore does not hold.

The converse holds too, so the lemma is the symmetry of stress said without coordinate axes. Take \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). Then \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) (definition 2.27), and (2.49) is exactly \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), the two pairs of shear forces on the cube. The lemma says the same for every pair of perpendicular cuts, not only for cuts perpendicular to the axes: the shear stress on the first plane in the direction of the normal of the second equals the shear stress on the second plane in the direction of the normal of the first. This is why we say that the shear stresses on perpendicular planes are equal in pairs. In the lectures the lemma is written in index form, which the button Index notation shows at (2.49), and the traction vector is written \(\vek t^{(\vek n)}\) there.

2.8.7 The inverse problem: a triangular piece

So far we have always gone the same way: we knew the stress components and computed the traction vector on a chosen plane by Cauchy's formula. Often the problem is posed the other way round. We know the forces on some faces of a piece and look for the stress components. Then we read Cauchy's formula as an equation for the unknown components. Let us show this on a triangular piece, on which we will at the end also check both conditions of equilibrium.

First a word that such a problem needs. The traction vector and the stress components belong to a point. A piece has many points, so we must say how the stress changes across it. In the figure there are marked points, in each the traction vector on a face with the same normal is drawn. On the left, at the hole, the vectors differ from point to point. In the middle they are the same everywhere. This is the simplest case: the stress does not change.

Definition 2.43 Homogeneous state of stress (homogeno napetostno stanje)

A body or a part of it is in a homogeneous state of stress (homogeneous state of stress, also uniform stress), when each of the nine stress components, written in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, has the same value at all of its points. A homogeneous state of stress is a property of the stress field in the body: the nine functions of the point are then nine constant numbers.

Source: LOVE art. 55 (PDF pp. 104-105), under the name uniform stress.

The word homogeneous means of the same kind, here the same everywhere. The definition mentions axes, but the property does not depend on them, since the same holds in turned axes: by Cauchy's formula (2.25) the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) for every normal \(\vek n\) is fixed by the three vectors \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\), \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\), \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\), and if these are the same at all points, so is \(\vek t(\vek n)\). We already know a homogeneous state of stress. In a bar pulled by an axial force the stress far from the ends is the same at all points (section 2.2), and likewise in the cube in pure shear (section 2.6.6), as in the plate in the middle. In the hanging bar, however, the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) grows toward the support, and the state is not homogeneous.

Now the problem. A thin steel sheet is pulled at its edges by forces in its plane. We cut a small triangular piece out of it in thought (figure 2.123).

We look at the piece along the axis \(z\), the axis \(x\) points right, the axis \(y\) up. We name its vertices \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). Side 3 is the segment \(AB\) on the axis \(x\), 20 mm long. Side 1 is the segment \(AC\), which rises from \(A\) at the angle \(45^\circ\) to the axis \(x\). Side 2 is the segment \(BC\), which rises from \(B\) to the left at the angle \(60^\circ\) to the axis \(x\). The sheet is \(d = 2\) mm thick in the direction of the axis \(z\), so each side in the figure is in fact a rectangular face of the height \(d\). Let two things be known:

\[\vek t(\vek n_1) = (-40,\ 10,\ 0)\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 40\ \text{MPa} .\]

The first is the traction vector on side 1, the force per unit area with which the rest of the sheet pulls the piece across this side. The second is one stress component. We look for the remaining stress components and for the traction vectors on sides 2 and 3. We chose the numbers ourselves. The model has three assumptions, and for each let us say why we may make it, when it fails and what it does to the result.

  1. The state of stress in the piece is homogeneous (definition 2.43). Why we may: the piece is small, and by step 4 of the proof of theorem 2.41 continuously differentiable stress components change over the distance \(h\) by at most \(G\,h\), so the less the smaller the piece. When not: next to a hole, a notch or a point force the stress changes strongly within a millimetre. What it does: the traction vector is the same at all points of a side, so the force on a side is exactly the traction vector times the area of the side, and Cauchy's formula holds for the whole piece, not only in the limit of a small tetrahedron.
  2. All stress components with the index \(z\) are zero. Why we may: nothing acts on the two large faces of the sheet, perpendicular to the axis \(z\), so there \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = \vek 0\), and by the symmetry (2.48) also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). The sheet is thin, so we assume this through the whole thickness. When not: in a thick piece or when something presses on a large face from outside. What it does: only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) remain, and all the traction vectors on the sides lie in the plane of the figure. In the lectures such a state is called a plane state of stress (ravninsko napetostno stanje), and we introduce it precisely in chapter 11.
  3. We leave out the weight. Why we may: by the equilibrium equations (2.38) the sum of the derivatives of the stress components and of the body force density is zero, and in a homogeneous state all the derivatives are zero, so the body force density must be zero too (LOVE art. 55, PDF p. 105). A homogeneous state and weight therefore do not go together, and one of the two is an approximation. What it does: the piece is \(12{,}68\) mm high, and the weight of steel would change the stress over this height by \(\rho g \cdot 12{,}68\ \text{mm} = 76\,518 \cdot 0{,}01268 = 970\) Pa, which is \(0{,}0024\ \%\) of 40 MPa. When not: in large bodies such as a tower or a dam, where the weight makes most of the stress.

Step 1: the outward normals from the figure. Cauchy's formula needs the outward normal of each side, the unit vector perpendicular to the side that points out of the piece (definition 2.17). For each side we first write the unit vector along it. Two unit vectors in the plane of the figure are perpendicular to the unit vector \((a, b, 0)\), namely \((b, -a, 0)\) and \((-b, a, 0)\), since its scalar product with each of them is \(a\,b - b\,a = 0\) (definition 2.11). We choose the one that points away from the piece.

side unit vector along the side the piece lies outward normal
1, \(AC\) \((\cos 45^\circ, \sin 45^\circ, 0)\) below right \(\vek n_1 = (-\sin 45^\circ, \cos 45^\circ, 0) = \big({-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, 0\big)\)
2, \(BC\) \((-\cos 60^\circ, \sin 60^\circ, 0)\) on the left \(\vek n_2 = (\sin 60^\circ, \cos 60^\circ, 0) = \big(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12, 0\big)\)
3, \(AB\) \((1, 0, 0)\) above \(\vek n_3 = (0, -1, 0)\)

The normal \(\vek n_1\) points up and left, \(\vek n_2\) up and right, \(\vek n_3\) down. We check the signs by computing: the vector from the vertex opposite a side to a vertex on the side runs across the piece toward the side, so its scalar product with the outward normal must be positive. For side 2 this is the vector \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (20, 0, 0)\) mm and \(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vek n_2 = 20 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 17{,}32\) mm, for side 1 the vector \(\overrightarrow{BA} = (-20, 0, 0)\) mm and \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\vek n_1 = 20 \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = 14{,}14\) mm, both positive.

Step 2: the two equations for the unknown components. The unknowns are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). The symmetry of stress (2.48) says \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so two remain, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). We write Cauchy's formula (2.27) for side 1, on which we know the traction vector, with \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\):

\[\begin{aligned} t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_1) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{1\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{1\mathrm{y}} : & -40 &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \cdot \Big({-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\Big) + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt2} , \\ t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n_1) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{1\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{1\mathrm{y}} : & 10 &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot \Big({-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\Big) + 40 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt2} . \end{aligned}\]

These are two linear equations for two unknowns, in megapascals. We solve them in three moves.

  1. We multiply the second equation by \(\sqrt2\): \(10\sqrt2 = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + 40\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 40 - 10\sqrt2 = 25{,}86\) MPa.
  2. We multiply the first equation by \(\sqrt2\): \(-40\sqrt2 = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + 40\sqrt2\).
  3. We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) from move 1: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 40 - 10\sqrt2 + 40\sqrt2 = 40 + 30\sqrt2 = 82{,}43\) MPa.

The stress components in the piece are therefore

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 82{,}43\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 40\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 25{,}86\ \text{MPa} .\]

What did the symmetry do here? Without it the first equation would hold \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) in place of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), a fourth unknown. The second equation would still give \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), but two unknowns would stay in the first, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and the problem would not have a single solution. The missing equation comes from the balance of moments, from which the symmetry follows.

Step 3: the traction vectors on the other two sides. Now we go the usual way again, from the components to the traction vector, by (2.27). On side 2 with the normal \(\vek n_2\)

\[\begin{aligned} t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_2) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{2\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{2\mathrm{y}} = 82{,}43 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + 25{,}86 \cdot \tfrac12 = 71{,}38 + 12{,}93 = 84{,}31\ \text{MPa} , \\ t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n_2) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{2\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{2\mathrm{y}} = 25{,}86 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + 40 \cdot \tfrac12 = 22{,}39 + 20 = 42{,}39\ \text{MPa} , \end{aligned}\]

and on side 3 with the normal \(\vek n_3 = (0, -1, 0)\)

\[t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_3) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot (-1) = -25{,}86\ \text{MPa} , \qquad t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n_3) = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot (-1) = -40\ \text{MPa} .\]

All three traction vectors point out of the piece, the first to the left, the second up and right, the third down and a little to the left: the rest of the sheet pulls the piece on all three sides. In the figure they are drawn to the same scale, and by (1.10) their sizes are \(41{,}23\) MPa, \(94{,}37\) MPa and \(47{,}63\) MPa.

Step 4: the forces add up to zero. The piece is at rest, so the resultant of the forces on it must be the zero vector ((2.2)). Let us check. By assumption 1 the force on a side is the traction vector times its area, the length of the side times the thickness \(d = 2\) mm. We get the lengths of sides 1 and 2 from the vertex \(C\). It lies on the line \(y = x\) through \(A\) and is \(L_2\) away from \(B\) in the direction \((-\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, 0)\), so \(C = (20 - \tfrac12 L_2,\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} L_2,\ 0)\) and \(20 - \tfrac12 L_2 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} L_2\). Hence \(L_2 = 40/(1 + \sqrt3) = 14{,}64\) mm, both coordinates of the vertex \(C\) are \(12{,}68\) mm, and \(L_1 = 12{,}68 \cdot \sqrt2 = 17{,}93\) mm. A megapascal is a newton per square millimetre (section 2.2), so we get the forces in newtons if we write the areas in mm². We computed with NumPy:

side length area \(t_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(t_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\)
1 \(17{,}93\) mm \(35{,}86\) mm² \(-40\) MPa \(10\) MPa \(-1434{,}5\) N \(358{,}6\) N
2 \(14{,}64\) mm \(29{,}28\) mm² \(84{,}31\) MPa \(42{,}39\) MPa \(2468{,}8\) N \(1241{,}4\) N
3 \(20\) mm \(40\) mm² \(-25{,}86\) MPa \(-40\) MPa \(-1034{,}3\) N \(-1600{,}0\) N
sum \(0{,}0\) N \(0{,}0\) N

In the right picture we draw the forces one after another. From the point \(S\) we draw the force \(\vek F_2\), at its tip we attach the force \(\vek F_1\) and to that the force \(\vek F_3\), which ends exactly at \(S\). The triangle of forces closes, which is the picture of the equation \(\vek F_1 + \vek F_2 + \vek F_3 = \vek 0\).

Is this the luck of these numbers? No, it closes for every homogeneous state. The reason is in the sides. The vector \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{i}}\), the length of a side times its outward normal, is the side turned by a quarter turn:

\[L_1\vek n_1 = (-12{,}68;\ 12{,}68)\ \text{mm} , \qquad L_2\vek n_2 = (12{,}68;\ 7{,}32)\ \text{mm} , \qquad L_3\vek n_3 = (0;\ -20)\ \text{mm} .\]

When we walk around the triangle from \(A\) over \(B\) and \(C\) back to \(A\), we return to the start, so the sum of the three side vectors is the zero vector. The same holds for all three turned by a quarter turn, and indeed \(-12{,}68 + 12{,}68 + 0 = 0\) and \(12{,}68 + 7{,}32 - 20 = 0\). By Cauchy's formula the component \(x\) of the sum of the forces is

\[d\,\big(L_1\,t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_1) + L_2\,t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_2) + L_3\,t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n_3)\big) = d\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\big(L_1 n_{1\mathrm{x}} + L_2 n_{2\mathrm{x}} + L_3 n_{3\mathrm{x}}\big) + d\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\big(L_1 n_{1\mathrm{y}} + L_2 n_{2\mathrm{y}} + L_3 n_{3\mathrm{y}}\big) = 0 ,\]

because both brackets on the right are zero, and likewise the component \(y\). This is the plane picture of the tetrahedron from section 2.6.2. There the areas of the three faces were \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\Delta A\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\Delta A\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\Delta A\) ((2.21)), which says the same: the areas times the outward normals add up to the zero vector. For the tetrahedron we derived Cauchy's formula from the balance of forces. Here we read the same relation the other way: where Cauchy's formula holds and the state is homogeneous, the first condition of equilibrium is fulfilled by itself.

Step 5: the forces do not turn the piece. The second condition of equilibrium (2.45) remains. The force is distributed evenly over each side, and the side is a rectangle of the length \(L_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the height \(d\), so by item 1 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force it turns the piece as if all of it acted at the midpoint of the side. We compute the moments about the vertex \(A\). The forces lie in the plane of the figure, so the moment has only the component \(z\), which by (2.39) equals \(x\,F_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\):

side midpoint \(x\,F_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\)
1 \((6{,}340;\ 6{,}340)\) mm \(6{,}340 \cdot 358{,}6 + 6{,}340 \cdot 1434{,}5 = 11\,368\) N mm
2 \((16{,}340;\ 6{,}340)\) mm \(16{,}340 \cdot 1241{,}4 - 6{,}340 \cdot 2468{,}8 = 4632\) N mm
3 \((10;\ 0)\) mm \(10 \cdot (-1600{,}0) - 0 = -16\,000\) N mm
sum \(0\) N mm

The sum is zero, the second condition is fulfilled. In the middle picture this is seen without computing. The lines of action of all three forces meet at one point, \(K = (13{,}02;\ 4{,}67)\) mm. About \(K\) every force has the lever arm zero and therefore the moment zero (lemma 2.38 on the lever arm and the magnitude of the moment). This is not luck either, but the symmetry of stress. If we computed all three traction vectors by Cauchy's formula with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = 20\) MPa instead of \(25{,}86\) MPa, the forces would still add up to zero, but the sum of the moments would be \(1485\) N mm. This is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\) times the area of the triangle \(126{,}8\) mm² and the thickness \(d\), much as for the cube the moment of the pairs was \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}})\,h^3\) in (2.46). The first condition of equilibrium is thus secured by Cauchy's formula, the second by the symmetry of stress.

What is worth taking away? Every known component of the traction vector on a plane with a known normal is one linear equation for the stress components. In the plane, with the symmetry taken into account, there are three unknowns, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so we need three data, here the two components of the vector \(\vek t(\vek n_1)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). In space there are six unknowns. In the lectures the same problem is posed on a triangle with one side on the axis \(y\), the normals are numbered in the same way, and Cauchy's formula is written as \(t_{\mathrm{i}}^{(\vek n)} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), with the order of the indices reversed, which by the symmetry is the same.

2.8.8 Pure shear again

Let us return to the cube in pure shear of section 2.6.6 (figure 2.64). The cube has the side \(s\), the axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, and the axis \(y\) into the picture, away from the viewer, so that the system is right-handed. We pull the top face to the right and the bottom face to the left with the force \(\tau_0\) per unit area. We pull the right face up and the left face down, now with the force \(\tau_1\) per unit area, and ask how large \(\tau_1\) must be. The first condition of equilibrium does not tell, since for every \(\tau_1\) the forces on the top and the bottom face are opposite, and so are the forces on the side faces.

The forces are distributed evenly over the faces, so by item 1 of lemma 2.40 on the moment of a distributed force each of them turns the cube as if it acted at the centre of its face. We put the origin at the centre \(P\) of the cube (figure 2.124). In the figure the axis \(x\) points right and the axis \(z\) up. The force on the top face is \(\tau_0 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the point \((0, 0, s/2)\), on the bottom face \(-\tau_0 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the point \((0, 0, -s/2)\), on the right face \(\tau_1 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((s/2, 0, 0)\) and on the left face \(-\tau_1 s^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((-s/2, 0, 0)\). By (2.39) their moments about \(P\) are

\[\begin{aligned} \Big(0, 0, \frac s2\Big)\times(\tau_0 s^2, 0, 0) &= \Big(0,\ \frac{\tau_0 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(0, 0, -\frac s2\Big)\times(-\tau_0 s^2, 0, 0) &= \Big(0,\ \frac{\tau_0 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(\frac s2, 0, 0\Big)\times(0, 0, \tau_1 s^2) &= \Big(0,\ -\frac{\tau_1 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) , \\ \Big(-\frac s2, 0, 0\Big)\times(0, 0, -\tau_1 s^2) &= \Big(0,\ -\frac{\tau_1 s^3}{2},\ 0\Big) . \end{aligned}\]

The sum is \(\big(0,\ (\tau_0 - \tau_1)\,s^3,\ 0\big)\). The second condition of equilibrium (2.45) requires it to be zero, so \(\tau_1 = \tau_0\). This is what we promised in section 2.6.6: the cube is in equilibrium exactly when all four forces per unit area are equally large. The moment of the pair on the top and the bottom face points in the direction of the axis \(y\), into the picture, and the viewer sees the cube turn clockwise. The moment of the pair on the side faces points out of the picture, and this pair turns the cube the other way. For \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa and \(s = 10\) mm the force on the top face is \(\tau_0 s^2 = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 5000\) N, and the moment of the pair is \(\tau_0 s^3 = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3 = 50\) N m. Without the forces on the side faces a moment of 50 N m would turn the cube.

In terms of stress components, \(\tau_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), the component \(x\) of the traction on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and \(\tau_1 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), the component \(z\) of the traction on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The condition \(\tau_1 = \tau_0\) is therefore \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), the symmetry of stress (2.48) in this example. On the ruler, two forces with zero resultant formed a pair that turns the ruler. On the cube in pure shear there are two such pairs, and they balance each other.

Theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress says that among the nine stress components at a point, which the cube with its coordinate axes shows, at most six are different: three normal ones, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and three shear ones, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) (SADD, PDF p. 79, EP, p. 54). The same is true of strain, which at a point is described by six numbers (definition 1.121). The reason, though, is different. For strain, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) holds by definition, because both are half of the same sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\). For stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) are components of forces on two different faces, and they are equal because of a law of mechanics, the second condition of equilibrium.

The table of the nine numbers of section 2.6.5, in which each row is one traction vector, is therefore symmetric about the diagonal:

\[\begin{array}{c|ccc} & x & y & z \\ \hline \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ \vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{array}\]

As a matrix (definition 1.94) it equals its transposed matrix, so it is symmetric (definition 1.103). For Cauchy's formula this means a simplification. By (2.27) we got the component \(x\) of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) from the column \(x\) of the table, \(t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Because of the symmetry the column equals the row of the same name, and

\[\begin{aligned} t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} , \\ t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} , \\ t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n) &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned}\]

With this the difference between our order of indices and that of CM, which exchanges the two indices (section 2.6.5), also disappears, since exchanging the indices does not change a stress component.

Of the three questions at the end of section 2.6.6 we have answered the last. The first two remain: how the six numbers change when we turn the axes, and on which face through the point the normal stress is largest and on which the shear stress. We take up the first in the next section, where we write the table of stress as a matrix and use it to turn the axes.
